response:
Please note, the recategorization process was performed for the balances as of December 31, 2023, for the 2024 ASR filing and the recategorized balances continued for future years. No specific recategorization occurred in 2025.
With the implementation of new accounting systems in 2022, all PS&I balances and transactions that were previously tracked through individual accounts based on the type of PS&I activity were merged into a single consolidated PS&I FERC sub account. During this transition, most of the data was converted with key identifiable information such as project number, description, and project organization in order to track the costs by the original category type. However, some existing PS&I costs were transferred without preserving identifiable information. As a result, categorizing transactions precisely within the PS&I account became significantly more difficult.
To address the categorization issue, each reconciler for various PS&I categories was tasked with reviewing and reconciling total PS&I transactions from 2022 through 2024. The review process included reviewing details from both the original and consolidated accounts for this time period. For transactions lacking segment data, reconcilers reviewed other sources such as payables, payroll, and journal entries to determine the correct category. Through the review of these sources, any identifiable transactions were re-categorized and/or new categories were added as reflected in the 2024 ASR. Any unidentified transactions that could not be tied to specific projects, in the amount of $27 thousand, were written off to expense in March 2025.

question: Do any of GPC’s outstanding long-term debt issues have call provisions?  If the answer is “yes,” please provide a list of the callable issues with the following: a) outstanding balance, b) issuance date, c) maturity date, d) coupon payment percent, e) annual interest expense, and f) call price (as a percent of par).
response:
Yes, $8.3 billion of Georgia Power’s outstanding long-term debt portfolio contain call provisions. Georgia Power routinely evaluates whether it is in the economic best interest of customers to call debt issuances. This regular monitoring of the debt portfolio is, in part, what leads to Georgia Power having a very low cost of debt, relative to peers. Most of Georgia Power’s long-term debt issues contain make-whole call, par call, or both make-whole and par call provisions.
Generally, it is uneconomic to call and replace debt via make-whole call provisions, which typically limit the issuer’s ability to refinance (even when interest rates fall). This is due to the fact that, in addition to the standard repayment of principal and accrued interest, make-whole calls also require the payment of an incremental fee (i.e., “make-whole premium”). The make-whole premium is the net present value of future coupon payments and principal, discounted at a rate equal to the sum of the make-whole spread and appropriate referencing benchmark Treasury yield. The call price is calculated in real time based on the appropriate reference benchmark Treasury yield. As a result of this incremental make-whole payment, bonds with make-whole call provisions are generally not economic to call and replace. Unlike bonds with make-whole provisions, bonds with par call provisions give the issuer the option to redeem the bonds at par on or after the call date, without paying an incremental premium to holders. As discussed in the Company’s response to STF-BAI-1-19, bonds that are callable at par are monitored for refinancing feasibility once they become callable, whereas bonds with make-whole call provisions are monitored based on market conditions.
Please see the below table for a detailed listing of Georgia Power’s long-term debt portfolio with call provisions, along with the information requested in this data request.
The call price for make-whole bonds fluctuates and is calculated in real time based on the appropriate referencing benchmark Treasury yield plus respective make-whole call spread. The call price of par call bonds is 100% of the notional amount.

question:
Has GPC performed any debt refinancing feasibility studies on its outstanding debt issues?  If the answer is “yes,” please provide the following:
A detailed description of the results from the study.
A detailed description of the conclusions(s) made by GPC based on the results of the study.
All debt refinancing feasibility studies in electronic format with all formulas intact.
response:
Georgia Power regularly monitors its debt portfolio for the opportunity to call debt and ultimately reduce costs to customers.
In the current debt portfolio, Georgia Power does not have any bonds outstanding that are callable at par. As stated in the Company’s response to STF-BAI-1-18, these types of refinancing feasibility studies are performed once the security reaches its respective par-call date.
For bonds with make-whole call provisions, Georgia Power actively monitors the feasibility of calling and replacing such bonds. The feasibility of a make-whole call is generally dependent on: (1) the interest savings from redeeming the bond prior to maturity less the make-whole premium (defined in the response to STF-BAI-1-18); and (2) the refinancing cost to replace the debt (if applicable). Generally, it does not make sense to take out existing debt with distant maturity dates via a make-whole call if it is immediately being replaced by a new issuance. Currently, all outstanding securities with make-whole calls require significant make-whole premiums to be paid (in addition to the repayment of principal plus accrued interest). As a result, it is currently more economical to take no action or wait until a security is callable at par when compared to a make-whole call.
In late 2021, Georgia Power completed a make-whole call analysis which identified a potential cost-saving opportunity on a bond with a near-term maturity. question:
Refer to “STF-JKA Informal Request - RTP Attachment TRADE SECRET.xlsb”
Please provide the historic split of day-ahead and hour-ahead sales by month for the past 10 years in the same format as on the “inputs” tab, columns H:M.   Please explain why the company believes the hour ahead and day ahead percentages will hold for the duration of the forecast period.
Refer to the day ahead and hour ahead RTP pricing provided in columns V:X.  Please explain how these prices were derived, and if they were derived at the monthly level.  If these prices were derived at the hourly level, please provide the hourly results.
Please explain what fuel/CO2/load forecast is utilized in these pricing results, and confirm that the load is consistent with the B22 forecast.  If these results were derived in an aurora run, please provide the archive file for the run including the .db, log, and all available output reports (resource year, resource month, zone native prices, etc.)
response:
Please see STF-JKA-5-7 Attachment A for the historic split of day-ahead and hour-ahead sales by month for years 2014 through 2021. Historical data at the requested level of detail prior to 2014 is not available.
The Company uses the most recent history available for the hour-ahead and day-ahead sales for purposes of calculating percentages for splitting day-ahead and hour-ahead sales by month. Historically, there has not a been a large deviation from year –to-year, although the monthly percentages may fluctuate slightly due to month-to-month kWh billing differences. The 3-year average of the historical splits are within +/- 0.5% of those used in the B2022 forecast, as referenced in STF-JKA Informal Request - RTP Attachment TRADE SECRET.xlsb, “inputs” tab, columns H:M.
Real Time Pricing (“RTP”) prices were derived at the monthly level by developing a monthly simple average utilizing the hourly forecasted RTP prices for the respective month. The hourly forecasted RTP prices are based on the components described in the pricing methodology section of the RTP tariff, which are projections of the hourly running cost of incremental generation (including approved environmental costs), provisions for losses, projections of hourly transmission costs and reliability capacity costs for each day (when applicable), and a recovery factor.
Please refer to the Company’s responses to STF-JKA-5-7 Attachments B and C for the day-ahead and hour-ahead RTP prices, respectively.
The fuel/CO2/load forecast is consistent with the Budget 2022 forecast.  Please refer to STF-JKA-5-7 Attachments D and E for the Aurora Energy Budget run.

question: Refer to “STF-JKA-1-2 Attachment M TRADE SECRET.xlsx” tab “Historical” row 348.  Please explain this significantly higher sales and revenue for October 2018.  Please provide any available memos, workpapers, and descriptions explaining this behavior.
response:
Fluctuations in historical load and revenues are normal and to be expected. Therefore, the Company does not ordinarily track or keep records for monthly variances. On a limited basis, and when determined appropriate, an observable variance may be investigated. In the case of the higher sales and revenue for October 2018, the Company did perform such an investigation and determined that the higher Governmental Lighting sales and revenue reported in October 2018 resulted from a billing delay with respect to a large customer from June through September 2018. The customer’s October bill included current and accumulated energy and revenue amounts for the months in which there was a billing delay, which resulted in higher sales and revenue numbers for the class in October 2018.
Please note that historical sales and revenues have no impact on the Governmental Lighting revenues used in the rate case for the test year or the years 2023-2025. A narrative of the method used to produce the Governmental Lighting energy and revenue forecasts has been provided in the Company’s response to STF-JKA-1-2 Attachment L.

The Company does not create its budget by simply applying an inflation factor to all the actual, or historic year, expenses. Expenses are reviewed and, based on known increases or decreases, the budget amounts are adjusted accordingly. Based on the type of expenditures, inflation rates may be applied to derive projected expenses.
Please see the Company’s response to STF-LA-2-6, which provides budget guidelines and assumptions for the 2022 budget process including escalation rates for both labor and non-labor costs (see “Escalation Rates” under Section III. Budget Details).
As provided in STF-LA-2-10 Attachment, the labor escalation rates are based on data supplied by the Employment Cost Index Private Sector Wages and Salaries and non-labor escalation rates are derived from the Bureau of Economic Analysis published GDP index values as of April 2022.

The Company funds the tax-qualified pension plan (“pension fund”) as required by law and when the Company deems contributions above required levels are appropriate. The Company contributes when required by law and annually assesses funding levels to determine if additional contributions will be made to the pension fund.
The prepaid pension asset represents the cumulative total net pension income (trust fund earnings less pension cost), plus pension contributions made by the Company, less pension obligation recognized to date. Under the Employee Retirement Income Security Act, the pension trust fund is not legally allowed to refund contributions or earnings to the Company. Accordingly, the Company records a prepaid pension asset to reflect prepaid contributions to the pension trust fund.
The prepaid pension asset provides earnings on the trust fund asset, which directly offsets the pension costs accrued by the Company. Therefore, the pension income serves to reduce the Company’s retail cost of service and revenue requirements for customers.
The prepaid pension asset has been included and accepted by the Commission as a component of retail rate base since it was first established in the 1991 base rate case. Since then, it has been reflected in the subsequent base rate cases and all annual and quarterly surveillance reports (“ASR”). These base rate cases and ASRs have also included the associated pension income from the prepaid pension asset.

Actual Account 925 expenses, in total and broken out by specific I&D type and category, for each year from 2016 through 2021, the 12-month period ended 6/30/2022, for the forecasted test year ending July 31, 2023 and for each forecasted calendar year 2022-2025.

In addition, explain how the Company accounts for such refunds and where these refunds are reflected in each of the annual I&D expenses to be provided in response to part a
response:
a. 	The Company assesses the need for an accrual for probable and reasonably estimable losses related to Injuries and Damages (I&D) claims and litigation monthly, debiting expense account 925 and crediting liability account 228.2, in accordance with Accounting Standards Codifications (ASC) 450 Contingencies, which states “an estimated loss from a loss contingency shall be accrued by a charge to income if both of the following conditions are met: (a) information available before the financial statements are issued indicates that it is probable that an asset had been impaired or a liability had been incurred at the date of the financial statements,” and “(b) the amount of loss can be reasonably estimated.” The balance in the reserve account represents the estimated value of claims outstanding and is adjusted monthly based on status of current or threatened litigations / claims. Actual costs associated with these potential claims and litigation are charged against the reserve. Account 925 includes these expense accruals associated with the I&D reserve, as well as other expenses related to workers compensation, safety and health, claims departments, and the costs of various liability insurance coverages.

f. Additionally, costs related to expected insurance reimbursements for certain legal matters from December 2016 through May 2022 were either recorded directly to account 143 as a receivable from the insurer or initially recorded to account 925 and reclassified to account 143.

question: Refer to Table C of the Company’s 2022 Selective Meter Test Report.  Please explain how the Company determines the number of meters to keep in stock for each meter strata.
response:
Table C in the Selective Meter Test Report refers to manufacturer and model as meter strata. This data is a good indicator of what manufacturer and model of meters are in the field, and it is very useful for tracking the accuracy trends across meter populations as is done in the Selective Meter Test Report. The data used to determine stocking levels includes more detailed information referred to as meter forms. Meter form is an American National Standards Institute (ANSI) standard. The form number provides information on what meter configurations should be set on certain service types. For instance, a form 2s meter is utilized on a 3 wire 120/240V service.
The number of meters to keep in stock is mainly dependent on the projected number of new customers, their service type, and system maintenance needs.

Due to the limitation of production at the REDACTED, Plants REDACTED and REDACTED have experienced reduced coal deliveries since August 2021. As a result, the Company has had to procure additional coal during this period in order to supplement the unfilled large coal commitment under contract with REDACTED. question: During 2020, 2021, and to-date in 2022, has GPC experienced disruptions in getting contracted coal supplies delivered to any of its generating plants?  If so, please identify and explain each such instance and also describe how that affected GPC 's coal inventory levels and GPC 's planning for and management of coal inventory at each of its plants.
response: During 2020 and through the first part of 2021, the Company experienced minimal disruptions in getting contracted coal supplies delivered to any of its generating plants. During that period, domestic coal demand was very weak and the Company’s plants maintained healthy inventories. The impact of COVID 19 and the accelerated emergence of wind and solar energy continued to apply downward pressure on coal markets and coal burns. Coal producers and transportation providers continued to downsize their organizations as they looked to a future with reduced coal demand. As gas prices started to increase toward the end of 2021, coal burns also started to increase. With an already tight coal supply, it became apparent that coal producers as well as transportation providers would be unable to meet the unanticipated rise in coal demand. As the fall of 2021 approached inventories at the Company’s plants began to decline as transportation providers continued to struggle to provide adequate service to maintain desired inventory levels. As a result, the Company began curtailing coal generation to conserve coal inventories at its plants in preparation for winter 2022 demand. As 2022 began, coal production remained constrained as labor and transportation issues for coal producers and transportation providers continued. Curtailment practices continued throughout the year to prepare for summer demand.  REDACTED.

question:
Will the Company be eligible to obtain any tax credits, or tax savings in 2022, 2023, 2024 or 2025 from the Inflation Reduction Act that was recently passed, such as, but not limited to, using renewable energy, reduced employee and retiree health care and prescription costs, or other provisions?
If not, explain fully why not.
If so, identify, quantify and explain all expected tax credits and tax savings benefits that the Company would be eligible for.
If different than the response to part b, identify, quantify and explain all benefits under the Act which the Company expects to claim for each year 2022, 2023, 2024 and 2025.
response:
The Company is continuing to evaluate the impacts of the Inflation Reduction Act (“IRA”). Based on the analysis completed thus far, the Company expects the IRA will provide tax benefits that, over time, can help reduce costs for customers. The Company will work with the Commission to determine which benefits best serve customers.
At this time, the Company has identified approximately $33 million of total potential benefits for 2022 through 2025 for the Commission’s consideration related to projected, qualified renewable and electric vehicle investments.  Listed below are the capital investments, along with estimated tax savings by year for 2022 through –2025, of the incremental benefits the Company has identified from the IRA, with related assumptions.

Solar Qualifying for Production Tax Credits | $ - | $ - | $ - | $ 32.7
EV Chargers | $ 2.0 | $ 3.0 | $ 3.0 | $ 3.0
Potential Tax Credits (in millions) | 2022 | 2023 | 2024 | 2025
Energy Storage Credits | $ - | $ 31.7 | $ - | $ -
Solar Credits | $ - | $ - | $ - | $ 0.4

Energy Storage Credits:  The IRA provides Investment Tax Credits (“ITC”) for standalone energy storage systems, no longer requiring it to be paired with and charged by solar generation. The Company believes the 65 MW Mossy Branch battery storage project, which is projected to be on-line in 2023, will qualify for a 30% ITC. The IRA also gives an “opt-out” from the existing ITC normalization, which permits the Company to recognize the full ITC benefit in the year the project goes into service, thereby providing a benefit to customers by lowering the levelized cost of electricity over the life of the project as compared to the cost under the existing ITC normalization option. In order to take advantage of this “opt out” option offered in the IRA, the Commission must specifically approve the “opt-out” option. The Company’s calculation above assumes that the full $31.7 million of estimated credit resulting from the normalization opt-out option would be recognized in 2025.
Solar Credits:  The IRA provides a PTC option, which may be utilized instead of the existing normalized ITC for solar investments. The Company estimates the PTC option will provide an approximate $0.4 million of additional benefits for customers in 2025 on projected self-build ash pond solar investments compared to the normalized ITC option.
EV Charger Credits: The IRA extends and modifies the credit for alternative fuel refueling property. This 30% ITC applies to property placed in service through 2032 and increases the credit limitation to $100,000 per EV charger. The Company is still required to normalize these ITCs over the life of the assets and expects an additional $0.8 million of total amortization in 2022-2025.
The Company is actively reviewing the wide range of flexible tax credits and other benefits from the IRA and, as such, the Company is still working on the analysis to be able to quantify further potential customer savings. For example, the Company’s evaluation of the IRA impacts on employee and retiree healthcare and prescription costs is in early stages and cannot be quantified at this time. Additionally, the Company is evaluating potential benefits for the Company’s electric vehicle purchases as well as the Hydro Modernization and Integrated Hydrogen Microgrid projects approved by the Commission in the 2022 IRP. Guidance is still needed to ensure proper implementations for all benefits, and the Company will continue to work with the Commission for customer impacts as it completes the analysis on these and any further identified benefits.

question: For each ash pond for which the Company is planning to remediate using a “closure in place” strategy please discuss and explain the risk of incurring additional costs if the “closure in place” method is determined to be inadequate to eliminate the contact of coal ash with groundwater.
response: With strict compliance deadlines for the closure of 29 ash ponds across the state, the Company must continue work on ash pond closures to meet the requirements in the federal and state CCR rules. Consistent with past practice, the Company plans and sequences work strategically to ensure closure progress continues as required in the shortest amount of time consistent with recognized and generally accepted good engineering practices (40 C.F.R. 257.102(d)(1)(v)), while also adjusting the schedule for certain activities to mitigate risk where possible. For example, where project work is underway or near complete, closure activities must continue to appropriately manage construction and environmental risk associated with safety, weather, compliance, and costs if the Company were to slow or stop work. For projects where primary closure construction work is not fully underway, to the extent possible and in light of mandatory closure timelines, the Company is mitigating risk by sequencing work to focus on site preparation, dewatering, and other construction activities that must be completed regardless of the closure option. In all cases, and at all ponds, the Company is executing plans, designed in consultation with third-party experts, to implement the Commission approved strategy to comply with the federal and state CCR rules.

question: Identify all costs, by account, incurred through December 31, 2021 for investigating and implementing beneficial use of coal ash.
response:
Beneficial use for this response is defined as the beneficial use of stored ash at the Company’s ash ponds and CCR landfills, as well as new research and technology associated with the beneficial use of stored coal ash.
The Company has invested $2.5 million through 2021 for investigating beneficial use of coal through the establishment of the Ash Beneficial Use Center (“ABUC”) at Plant Bowen in partnership with EPRI and other utilities. These costs were recorded to FERC account 506 in December 2018.
Beneficial use is being implemented for the ash pond closures at Plant Mitchell. All costs and benefits associated with the closure of Mitchell’s three ash ponds are applied to the Company’s coal combustion residuals asset retirement obligation (“CCR ARO”). As outlined in STF-PIA-10-13 Attachment A in the Company’s response to STF-PIA-10-13, there has been $65 million in total costs incurred at Plant Mitchell through December 31, 2021 to close the ash ponds by removal, which includes, but is not limited to, costs associated with project engineering, planning, site preparation, and ash excavation. Of the total costs incurred through December 31, 2021 at Plant Mitchell, payments to third parties specifically for transportation and contractor costs associated with beneficial use, excluding excavation costs, total approximately $11 million. The $11 million spent on beneficial use activities to support the closure by removal for Plant Mitchell would otherwise be forecasted for transportation and disposal costs if the ash was not being beneficiated.
Finally, Georgia Power initiated a request for proposals (“RFP”) for beneficial use of stored coal ash in late 2019. The beneficial use RFP process was supported by Company experts and third-party engineering consultants with activities such as the development of site information and ash quality data, as well as the detailed evaluation of bid proposals received. Total costs incurred through December 31, 2021 for site investigations, package preparations, and other analysis activities are approximately $1.3 million. These costs were accounted for under the Company’s CCR ARO.

Did the Company consider developing and applying any criteria for selecting sites where it will invest in Community Charging sites? If so, please identify and explain the criteria. If not, explain fully why not.

Show in detail how the criteria provided in response to part a has been applied to each candidate site that Company has already identified.

response:
a. Yes, the Company takes several inputs into consideration when determining a new site location: customer interest; other EV charging service providers’ plans; and alignment with the Community Charging program design. Customer interest is identified based on outreach from and to customers and communities including cities and municipalities as well as retail establishments. Publicly available information such as the PlugShare EV Charging Station Map (www.plugshare.com) provides some information regarding future plans of other EV charging service providers. Combining customer interest with expected public fast charging gaps for EV motorists in the state are precursors for evaluating a potential new site before reviewing site-specific information through the process described below.
Once the general location of a prospective new site is identified, the Company considers site-specific information to identify and select a specific location. To help in final site identification, the Company developed three major categories with weighting measures and ratings (1-3) with 3 as the highest. An overall weighted score of 2 or higher qualifies as a prospective new EV charging site through this process. The criteria require new EV charging sites installed through the Community Charging program must be safe, accessible, and equitable.
Safe: EV drivers need to feel safe when they are charging. Criteria in this category include visibility from the roadway, presence of secure & sufficient lighting, and the operating hours of the business location.
Accessible: EV drivers need sites to be accessible for EV charging. Criteria in this category include proximity to travel corridors and amenities as well as whether the charger itself would be publicly accessible at all times.
Equitable: Within reasonable expectation, new EV charging sites should not interfere with other public charger networks and should meet a public need for EV charging without creating excessive costs for installation. Criteria in this category include proximity to other existing or anticipated public direct current (DC) fast charging sites, the income-level of the community where the new site would be located, and the cost to serve the site.

question: Please provide a detailed description of the application process for customers interested in enrolling in the Make Ready program. Please describe all relevant eligibility and participation requirements, and provide a copy of the current draft versions (or finalized versions, if available) of the program manual, terms and conditions, or other program guidance documents.
response:
The application process for customers begins when a Georgia Power customer completes an online application designed to capture enough information about the customer and potential electric transportation infrastructure project requirements to allow the Company to begin an assessment of the project. Below is an overview of the process:
Application: Participant applies online providing necessary details to help the Company evaluate eligibility of the application and the needs of the project, such as site location address, phone number and contact information, Georgia Power account number, number and type of preferred charging ports (if known), and other useful documents specific to the customer’s project site.

Program Participation Finalized: The customer accepts and provides signature to approve the final project plan.
Construction: Make Ready infrastructure is installed and energized by the Company, and the customer completes installation of customer-owned charging equipment.
Utilization: Make Ready infrastructure is maintained by the Company. The charging equipment is maintained by the customer or their designated third party.
The program is available to all existing Georgia Power commercial and industrial customers. Multi-family properties are also eligible as defined by their commercial rate. There are exceptions to participation as noted in the Company’s standards document.
Make Ready dollars will not be used to cover electric vehicle (“EV”) mandates in place by city ordinance.
Make Ready dollars are not available to third party EV charging service provider companies locating on a site host’s property.
Make Ready dollars are available to car dealerships only to the extent that the car dealership’s project scope includes a public charging benefit.

question:
Refer to the direct testimony of witness Legg at page 17, lines 6-8, which states that “Participation in Charge It is available to new, separately metered charging loads that are served on Georgia Power’s system after January 1, 2023.”
Please explain why the Company does not propose to make the Charge It-EV rider available to existing charging stations with a rolling 12-month load factor below 15%.
Could the Charge It EV program have a higher level of participation if it were to also be made available to existing charging stations with a rolling 12-month load factor below 15%?  If not, explain fully why not.
response:
The Charge It rider (CIEV-1) was designed to encourage new investment in EV charging infrastructure. The program was evaluated on a marginal basis and only considered incremental load to our system and the associated revenues. Existing customers who have already made these investments presumably did so based upon the electricity rates available at that time; therefore, the new Charge It rider is not necessary to support their economic analysis. Additionally, offering the Charge It rider to existing customers would result in a cost shift with non-participating customers having to make up the difference. In addition, the CIEV tariff passed the Rate Impact Measure (“RIM”) test, which indicates that the proposed tariff will ultimately lower rates for all customers.
It is possible that participation may be higher if the rider was made available to existing charging stations if they met all of the other applicability requirements of the tariff. However, this would be inappropriate and contrary to the intent of the rider to encourage new investment and expand charging infrastructure beyond what is currently in place.

question:
Identify the quantity of RECs that the Company projects for each of these periods: (1) calendar 2022; (2) the future test year; and (3) each plan year, 2023 through 2025.
Please also identify and explain each program that requires the Company to retire RECs.
Please identify the quantity of RECs for each period that is being used for each program that requires the retirement of such RECs and explain how RECs are being retired for each such program.
response:
The table below reflects projected RECs to be retired by each program for the specified time periods. The RECs will be generated from Company-owned renewable assets, acquired through renewable purchased power agreements, or purchased in the wholesale market. One REC is equal to one MWh of electricity.
NOTE: REC inventory is quantified on an annual basis and not a monthly basis, therefore the following calculation was used to estimate test period amounts: 5/12 (2022) + 7/12 (2023).
Summaries of each customer program are provided below.
Programs Requiring REC Retirement on behalf of Participant Customers
C&I REDI (2016 IRP) designed to allow existing Commercial and Industrial customers to subscribe to renewable energy procured by Georgia Power. In return, the customer receives hourly credits based on its pro-rata share of energy produced from a portfolio of renewable facilities up to 200 MW.
Clean and Renewable Energy Subscription (CARES) (2022 IRP) allows Commercial and Industrial​ customers to support their sustainability initiatives and renewable energy goals by subscribing to the output from 2,100 MW of additional renewable generation Georgia Power will procure through two RFPs.
Carbon Free Energy/Around The Clock (CFE/ATC) - an option under the CARES program that allows customers to subscribe to ≤ 100 MW of carbon free energy that will be available around the clock, supplied by ≤ 650 MW of solar and a Battery Energy Storage System.
Customer-Connected Solar Program (CCSP) (2019 IRP) allows existing Commercial and Industrial customers to partner with solar developers to build a solar facility on or adjacent to the customers’ property. Georgia Power will purchase 100% of the energy generated.​
Community Solar (2019 IRP) allows Residential customers the opportunity to support the development of solar power in Georgia by subscribing to a portion of the generation provided by local solar farms. For a fixed price per block, participating customers receive energy credits on their monthly bill based on the solar farms’ production. The program will be eligible for Commercial (GS) rates beginning in 2023.
Company-owned facilities are developed by Georgia Power for the benefit of all customers.
Customer Renewable Supply Procurement (CRSP) (2019 IRP) allows Commercial & Industrial​ customers to support their sustainability initiatives and renewable energy goals by subscribing to the output from 1,000 MW of renewable generation.
Retail REC Retirement (R3) (2022 IRP) allows customers to support their sustainability initiatives and aggressive renewable energy goals by subscribing to renewable generation previously procured by Georgia Power through PPAs. Participating customers pay a fixed price per kWh. Existing customers with load > 15MW and incremental new load > 50MW are eligible to participate.
Simple Solar (2016 IRP) allows customers the ability to support the growth of solar energy while reducing their electric-based carbon footprint. For an additional fee per kWh, customers can match either 50% or 100% of their monthly energy usage with RECs. RECs are sourced from solar facilities and purchased on the wholesale market. All customers are eligible to participate.
Flex REC (2022 IRP) allows customers the ability to support the growth of renewable energy while reducing their electric-based carbon footprint. For an additional fee per kWh, customers can match up to 100% of their annual energy usage with RECs. RECs are sourced from solar, wind, and potentially other renewable resources, and purchased on the wholesale market. Commercial and Industrial customers requiring a minimum of 100,000 kWhs of RECs are eligible to participate.
Income Qualified Community Solar (IQCS) (2022 IRP) pilot program allows corporate sponsors to buy down the Community Solar program’s monthly subscription cost to increase affordability and provide renewable energy to income-qualified customers.​ Corporate sponsors fund 75% of the monthly subscription plus shared administrative costs; RECs are retired on their behalf​. The remaining 25% of the subscription cost is paid by participating customers who will receive energy credits on their monthly bill based on the solar farms’ production. ​The program is available to up to 5,000 income-qualified customers on a first-come, first-served basis.

question:
August 2022 plant retirements and related amortization. Refer to the response to STF-LA-2-15 and specifically the STF-LA-2-15 Attachment.  As it relates to (1) Plant Wansley Units 1-2, (2) Plant Wansley Unit 5a CT and Plant Boulevard CT, page 1 of the attachment includes “Note a” which states: “These projected accounts have not been set up yet; proposed amortization will begin in January 2023.”  However, this attachment shows the following amortization amounts for each month October through December 2022: (1) Plant Wansley Units 1-2 - $4.831 million, (2) Plant Wansley Unit 5a CT - $18,000, and (3) Plant Boulevard CT – ($14,000).
Please explain and reconcile this discrepancy.  Identify, quantify and explain each reconciling item.
Show what the depreciation expense would have been for each unit for each month August – December 2022 had it not been retired in August 2022.
Starting at in January 2023, the amortization amounts increase as follows: (1) Plant Wansley Units 1-2 from $4.831 million to $5.808 million, (2) Plant Wansley Unit 5a CT from $18,000 to $20,000, and (3) Plant Boulevard CT from ($14,000) to ($26,000).  Please explain fully the reasons for these amortization amounts changing and show how they were derived.  Show detailed calculations.
For the Plant Wansley Units 1-2 regulatory asset, please identify the related monthly ADIT amounts for the test year and each calendar year 2022, 2023, 2024 and 2025 and show how such amounts were derived.  Show detailed calculations.
For the Plant Wansley Unit 5a CT regulatory asset, please identify the related monthly ADIT amounts for the test year and each calendar year 2022, 2023, 2024 and 2025 and show how such amounts were derived.  Show detailed calculations.
For the Plant Boulevard CT regulatory asset, please identify the related monthly ADIT amounts for the test year and each calendar year 2022, 2023, 2024 and 2025 and show how such amounts were derived.  Show detailed calculations.
response:
“Note a” included in STF-LA-2-15 Attachment for the net book values of retired plants is incorrect and should have read “[T]hese projected accounts have not been set up yet; proposed amortization will begin in October 2022.”, which reconciles to the projected amortization of the net book values in the STF-LA-2-15 Attachment.
Had the plants not been retired, the projected monthly depreciation expense for Plants Wansley Units 1-2, Wansley Unit 5a CT, and Boulevard CT for the remainder of the year would have been $4,831 thousand, $18 thousand, and $14 thousand, respectively. The amounts for Plants Wansley Units 1-2 and Wansley Unit 5a CT reconcile to the projected amortization expenses of the net book values in STF-LA-2-15 Attachment. The projected monthly amortization expense for Plant Boulevard CT was inadvertently reflected as a negative $14 thousand instead of a positive $14 thousand in the filing, as shown in STF-LA-2-15 Attachment. Please note, the plants were assumed to be retired in September 2022 in the 2022 rate case budget and therefore, a depreciation expense is recorded for September 2022 instead of an amortization expense. However, the net book value is amortized at the same rate as the depreciation expense for the remainder of 2022 and therefore, there is no impact to retail cost of service or retail rate base.
As ordered in the 2022 IRP, Docket No. 44160, the amortization expense upon retirement until December 2022 reflects the amounts the units would have otherwise been depreciated based on their depreciation rates approved in the Company’s 2019 base rate case. The amortization expense starting in January 2023 is a calculation of the projected remaining net book values as of December 2022 divided ratably over the respective amortization periods.
d-f. Please see STF-LA-11-2 Attachment for the ADIT amounts related to the regulatory asset for remaining net book values of Plants Wansley Units 1-2 and Wansley Unit 5a CT, and the regulatory liability for remaining net book value of Plant Boulevard CT. The ADITs are calculated using the combined federal and state tax effect of those balances at 25.47%.

question: Reference p. 5, l. 11-15. question: Reference p. 7, l. 19-21.  Please define “reasonable ROE”.  Specifically, is a “reasonable ROE” 10.50%, 10.00%, 9.50%, 9.00%, 8.50%?  Please be as specific as possible and provide a range of “reasonable” ROEs.
response:
As explained in Mr. Coyne’s Direct Testimony, a “reasonable ROE” is one that satisfies the three standards established by the U.S. Supreme Court in two bellwether decisions by the United States Supreme Court, notably Bluefield Waterworks and Improvement Company v. Public Service Commission of West Virginia, 262 U.S. 679 (1923) (“Bluefield”), and Federal Power Commission v. Hope Natural Gas Company, 320 U.S. 591 (1944). In those decisions, the Supreme Court determined that a just and reasonable return is one that is: (1) commensurate with returns on investments in enterprises having comparable risks; (2) adequate to attract capital on reasonable terms, thereby enabling the utility to provide safe, reliable service; and (3) sufficient to ensure a utility’s financial soundness.
A “reasonable” ROE, therefore, enables the Company to finance capital expenditures (using both debt and equity) on favorable financing terms and provide it with the ability to raise capital under a full range of capital market circumstances.
Because the cost of equity is expectational and premised on the principle of opportunity costs, it cannot be precisely quantified. Moreover, as the Supreme Court stated in Bluefield, “a rate of return may be reasonable at one time and become too high or too low by changes affecting opportunities for investment, the money market and business conditions generally.” In other words, a reasonable ROE reflects current and expected capital market conditions that the subject utility faces, as well as investors’ expectations and requirements regarding both risks and returns.
Mr. Coyne’s 11.00 percent ROE recommendation, which includes flotation costs, is based on the average ROE estimate for his risk comparable proxy group developed through four analytical approaches that apply current and projected economic and financial market data. In Mr. Coyne’s opinion, 11.00 percent, which is the mean, or central tendency of the results from all models, best reflects the investor required return under current and expected economic and capital market environment for a utility of similar risk to Georgia Power.

question: Please explain how the DOE loans as noted in S-9 are priced and the corresponding yields are determined. Is credit a factor in the pricing of those loans? Please fully explain the answer.
response:
Yes, the 0.375% spread to Treasuries that was negotiated with the DOE incorporated the company’s credit profile. All DOE loans were priced at an interpolated treasury rate + 0.375%. Calculated by the DOE for each draw, the interpolated treasury rates were derived by computing the present value of an interpolated treasury curve matching the weighted average life for each draw on the draw date.  Therefore the price, dependent upon treasury rates, varied based on the market conditions at the time of the draws, but the 37.5 basis point spread was fixed for all draws, regardless of tenor or credit rating.
For example, the weighted average life for the $329 million 12/10/2020 draw was 15.68 years on the draw date. The underlying treasury rate for this draw was 1.362%, which equaled the interpolated 15.68yr treasury rate based on the treasury yield curve one business day prior to the draw. Adding the fixed 37.5 basis points to 1.362% resulted in the final interest rate of 1.737% for this draw.

response: Non-subscribing customers benefit from the NU-1 tariff through subscriber payments collected through the tariff in exchange for the carbon free attributes generated by the uprate projects. question: What happens to the incremental revenue from the NU-1 tariff? Identify and explain the accounting treatment for all revenue and expenses associated with the tariff. Does this accounting treatment differ from what is required by accounting standards? Regarding the proposed accounting treatment, what specifically does Georgia Power have to receive approval from the Commission?
response:
The Company is proposing to collect revenues under the NU-1 tariff associated with the nuclear uprate project in two ways.
The Program Enrollment Contribution (“PEC”) will be collected from subscribers prior to the in-service date of the Plant Hatch uprate project and will be recognized as a prepaid liability under the accounting guidelines. The prepaid revenue will be amortized over the assumed remaining life of the asset to other operating revenues, which will reduce retail cost of service for retail customers. The Company does not require separate approval from the Commission for this accounting treatment. However, as discussed with Staff and per the Company's Application for Approval of the 2026 Plant Hatch Units 1-2 Nuclear Extended Power Uprates, the Company is requesting Commission approval for the following accounting treatment. For any PEC payments received from the tariff subscribers in 2028, the Company will apply the payments to CWIP base in 2028 solely for the purposes of calculating AFUDC on the project and the payment will be excluded from retail rate base. Beginning in 2029, any PEC payments will be applied as a reduction to retail rate base following GAAP accounting and will be reflected as such in the 2028 base rate case projections. In the event the current Alternate Rate Plan (“ARP”) is extended beyond 2028, any further application of the PEC payments to CWIP base shall be considered as part of the ARP extension.
The Zero Emission Credit (“ZEC”) revenue will be collected from subscribers once the nuclear uprate is in-service and recognized as collected under the accounting guidelines. This revenue will be recorded to other operating revenues and reduce retail cost of service for retail customers. The Company does not require separate approval from the Commission for this accounting treatment. However, as discussed with Staff and per the Company's Application for Approval of the 2026 Plant Hatch Units 1-2 Nuclear Extended Power Uprates, the Company is requesting Commission approval for the following accounting treatment. Any ZEC payments received from the tariff subscribers through December 31, 2028, will be recorded as a regulatory liability until the next base rate case. If the ARP is further extended, deferral of ZEC payments beyond 2028 will be considered as part of the terms of the extension. Beginning January 1, 2029, any ZEC payments received from the tariff subscribers will be trued-up on an actual basis to the projected amounts included in the next base rate case.
In order to mitigate revenue requirement impacts to non-subscribing customers before the full benefits of uprated capacity can be realized, the Company is requesting approval from the Commission to defer depreciation and interest expenses associated with the Plant Hatch project capital cost closed to plant in service. The deferred depreciation and interest expenses are proposed to be amortized over the life of the asset once the project is complete and uprate projects reach commercial operation date (“COD”). Amortization of the deferred depreciation and interest would begin in the month the incremental uprate capacity is placed in service and begins generating incremental electricity through the end of the life of the units, aligning cost recovery with the start of incremental generation and the associated project benefits.

question: Regarding proposed uprate ZEC program, please explain whether the Company is proposing a standalone, distinct program specific to nuclear uprates, or if this represents an expansion of the existing Flex-REC program.  Compare and Contrast the proposed program to the Flex-REC program and identify limitations with the Flex-REC program.
response:
The Nuclear Uprate Subscription program is proposed to be a standalone program and not an expansion of the Flex-REC program, which is a program that offers access to attributes from renewable energy resources. There are several differences between the proposed Nuclear Uprate Subscription program and the Flex-REC program listed below.
The Nuclear Uprate Subscription program allows for a 25-year term, which permits the customer and Georgia Power to lock in long-term fixed prices for the Zero Emissions Credits (ZECs). In contrast, the Flex-REC program only allows for a maximum 3-year term and is based on market prices, which can fluctuate over time.
The Nuclear Uprate Subscription program allows for hourly matching of ZEC production and customer energy consumption since the ZECs are created by baseload nuclear units. Whereas, the Flex-REC program only procures solar RECs produced during daylight hours, which do not necessarily align with the customer’s energy consumption.  The customer interested in participating in the ZEC program is seeking to support resources that produce clean energy that aligns with their energy use.
The revenue from the Nuclear Uprate Subscription program will reduce rates for customers while the Flex-REC program is simply a pass-through for the actual costs to procure the RECs. Additionally, a portion of the revenue from the Nuclear Uprate Subscription program will be realized during the construction period to offset some of the cost of the uprates, preceding the delivery of ZECs. The Flex REC program bills monthly as RECs are delivered.

question: The 2026 CBA model separates baseline capital from incremental capital, showing incremental costs extending through the end of the plant's life. This contrasts with the 2025 IRP, which showed a planned spending offset from 2031–2039 and zero incremental capital thereafter. response:
There has been no accounting change made to the B26_AV_TOOL_HatchEPU workbook (“B26 AVTool”) relative to the 2025IRP_AV_Nuclear TRADE SECRET TN STAFF (“’25IRP AVTool”).  Rather, when inspecting the cost sheets in both of the tools, be aware that the data is being input differently.  In the 25IRP AVTool, a consolidated EPU budget spend curve was entered into the cost sheet and the tool calculated revenue requirements.  In the current iteration of the economics, the choice was made to utilize the Standard Analysis Model (“SAM”) to generate revenue requirements, not only to enhance the accuracy of the revenue requirements which are now calculated at the individual asset level, but also to help process other inputs like the customer prepayment and regulatory deferral.  SAM takes the individual asset spend curves and creates individual revenue requirements that are aggregated as an output of that tool and input directly into the cost sheet of the B26 AVTool.  Because the revenue requirements have already been generated the AVTool doesn’t need to calculate them which is why when trying to compare the cost sheet from the different tools, it will look different even though the project has not changed substantively from the budget perspective.  The B26 AVTool may look like it has incremental capital after the construction period but that isn’t the case, and those dollars are representative of the revenue requirements.
All assets including projects subject to advancement can be seen individually in SAM on the Input_Output sheet.

question:
Refer to the response to STF-LA-2-71.  Please explain the costs related to the following Accounts:
Employee Pension and Benefits – SERP
Employee Pension and Benefits – SERP Non-Service Cost
Employee Pension and Benefits – Service Awards
Employee Pension and Benefits – Recreation
response:
Supplemental Executive Retirement Plan (“SERP”) costs are service costs related to the Southern Company SERP and Supplemental Benefit Plan (SBP–Pension), which are nonqualified pension benefits for senior management level employees. The service costs represent the increase in the projected benefit obligation resulting from an additional year of service provided by the eligible employee.
SERP Non-Service Cost are related to the non-service cost portion of SERP and SBP-Pension and represent interest costs, amortization of prior service costs, and any gains or losses from prior years.
Service Awards costs represent awards provided to employees based on various years of service.
Recreation costs represent miscellaneous meals and travel expenses. These costs were inadvertently budgeted to Employee Pension and Benefits account 926-00350 and should have been budgeted to Office Supplies and Expenses account 921-00000.

question: Refer to the response to STF-LA-2-72.  Please explain the decreases in the Contract Labor from $448.492 million in the test year period to $363.444 million through the rate year 2025 period.  How is Contract Labor allocation among the Southern Company regulated subsidiaries?
response:
The decrease in projected contract labor O&M expenses from $448.492 million in 2022 to $363.444 million in 2025 is largely driven by decreases in contract labor related to steam generation, transmission, and distribution functions. The projected decrease in steam generation contract labor is primarily driven by lower outage spend in 2024 and 2025 as well as projected steam unit retirements. The projected decrease in distribution contract labor is primarily driven by lower vegetation management spend and the completion of the distribution backlog in 2022. The projected decrease in transmission contract labor is primarily driven by lower asset management spend due to current and forecasted economic conditions.
The contract labor O&M expenses reflected in the Company’s response to STF-LA-2-72 exclude SCS contract labor billed to Georgia Power. SCS contract labor costs are allocated to affiliate companies using cost allocation methods based on the services performed.

question: Refer to the response to STF-LA-2-73.  Please provide the Company’s vacancy rate ratio for the periods 2017 – 2021.  How did the Company determine the budgeted headcount of as of May 2022 of 6,546 and 7,016 beginning in June 2022 through 2025, respectively?
response:
Actual vacancy rates at the end of each year from 2017 through 2021 are provided below.
 | 2017 | 2018 | 2019 | 2020 | 2021
Vacancies at Year-End | 781 | 430 | 455 | 668 | 706
Vacancy Rate % of Total Budget | 10% | 6% | 6% | 9% | 10%
Vacancies occur throughout the year and will fluctuate from month to month. The process for posting and filling vacancy positions takes time to complete. If a job is filled internally, the vacancy moves to a different business unit and the process of filling it starts over again. Additionally, attrition rates are on the rise and replacing positions externally has been challenging with the current competitive labor market. The Company continues to focus on attracting and retaining talent to ensure safe, reliable service for its customers. However, in the interim when vacancies are not filled, work is performed by utilizing overtime from existing workforce and contract labor.
The headcount of 6,546 positions referenced in the question was the actual headcount in May 2022. Annually, Human Resources works with the business units to align staffing plans with individual business unit work plans. The budgeted headcount is based on these expected business unit staffing plans and represents the estimated positions the Company needs in order to function efficiently and effectively to meet operational and customer needs. Based on that process as outlined, the Company budgeted a headcount of 7,016 positions for years 2022 through 2025. The actual headcount in May 2022 does not include the approximately 470 vacancies the Company was unable to fill at that time.

question: As referenced in 1 above, please provide the reasonings for increases in each of the Production Expenses from the filed petition dated June 24, 2022 to the Supplemental filing dated August 22, 2022 for the rate years 2023-2025.  Please explain why the Test Year expenses did not change in the Supplemental Filing.   (Include Total Electric and Adjusted Electric and Wholesale and Retail)
response:
The changes in Production Expenses in the 2022 Base Rate Case Supplemental Filing are due to the outcome of the 2022 IRP, as approved by the Commission in its final order in Docket No. 44160. Below is a list of the items that impacted production expenses.
The Commission’s deferral of the retirement decision for Plant Bowen Units 1 and 2 resulted in an increase in 2023-2025 for Total Electric, Adjusted Electric, and Retail Production Expenses.
The four DER Local Reliability and Constraints Pilot Projects approved by the Commission were not included in the Company’s rate case filing on June 24, 2022, which resulted in an increase in 2024 and 2025 for Total Electric, Adjusted Electric, and Retail Production Expenses.
The Capacity RFP Additional Sum was reduced by the Commission, which resulted in a decrease in 2024 and 2025 for Adjusted Electric and Retail Production Expenses in 2024 and 2025.
DG PPA Additional Sum approved by the Commission was not included in the Company’s rate case filing on June 24, 2022, which resulted in an increase in 2025 for Adjusted Electric and Retail Production Expenses.
The Wholesale to Retail Offer was rejected by the Commission which resulted in a decrease in 2024 and 2025 for Retail Production Expenses (Wholesale Production Expenses increased).
The Test Year Production Expenses in the Supplemental Filing inadvertently did not include an increase related to Plant Bowen Units 1 and 2 O&M of $4.9 million in Total Electric, Adjusted Electric, and Retail as a result of the Commission deferring a retirement decision on these units. This correction will increase the Company’s test period revenue requirement deficiency by $4.9 million. However, there is no resulting impact to the Company’s levelized revenue requirement request in the 2022 Base Rate Case Supplemental Filing.

The number of customers that have contacted the Company regarding TOU-RD is not tracked, and as a result there is also not a summary of the complaints related to the TOU-RD rate. Based on feedback from the Company’s Customer Service organization, there does not seem to be a disproportionate number of calls, concerns, or complaints related to the TOU-RD rate when compared to the Company’s other residential rate offerings.

question: Please provide informational materials provided to customers of new residential premises related to the default rate (TOU-RD).
response:
New customers to the Smart Usage rate (TOU-RD) receive a welcome letter that confirms their enrollment and provides helpful information to educate them on how to take advantage of the rate’s design. This information is provided to all customers who enroll in the rate – regardless of whether they reside at a newly established premises or at an existing premises. This information is provided via email if an email address is available; otherwise, it is provided by direct mail.
Additionally, customers enrolled in Smart Usage receive multiple seasonal postcards that highlight the on and off-peak pricing differences. The message includes specific reminders to shift usage to capitalize on the TOU design as well as emphasizing the importance of managing demand.
The materials provided also encourage customers to visit the Georgia Power website for more information on the Smart Usage rate and for tips on managing their energy usage.

question:
Please refer to Womack testimony on page 6 lines 19 – 24 and page 7 lines 17 - 22.
Over the last ten years, the Company has invested approximately $9.7 billion in transmission and distribution infrastructure to strengthen the reliability and resiliency of our network for the benefit of customers. This includes approximately $4.9 billion invested in transmission and distribution infrastructure since January 2020 and projected through December 2022, which includes $1.5 billion for investments in the Company’s Grid Investment Plan.
With the Company’s 2022 base rate case, Georgia Power seeks to build upon this progress by continuing to invest in its transmission and distribution system to provide safe and reliable electric service to its customers. Based on projections for 2023 through 2025, the Company will invest an additional $6.8 billion in transmission and distribution improvements, which will include $2.2 billion in continued investment in the Company’s Grid Investment Plan.
a. The Company invested $4.8 billion in T&D during the seven-year period through December 2019 or $700 million per year. The Company invested $4.9 billion since January 2020 and projected through December 2022 or $1.6 billion per year. The Company proposes to invest $6.8 billion in T&D or $2.3 billion per year during the period January 2023 through December 2025. Please explain the necessity of increasing annual T&D investment by 44 percent from current three-year accounting order period (2020 – 2022) of $1.6 billion per year and 230 percent from prior accounting periods (2013 – 2019) of $700 million per year. Specifically, could the Company continue to invest approximately $1.0 to $1.5 billion per year and still provide safe and reliable service? Please answer yes or no, and then provide any explanation.
b. How much of the $4.9 billion T&D capital investment during 2020 - 2022 was necessary to address direct safety issues as opposed to reliability issues?
c. How much of the proposed $6.8 billion T&D capital investment for 2023 – 2025 is necessary to address direct safety issues as opposed to reliability issues?
d. How much of the $4.9 billion T&D capital investment during 2020 - 2022 was to address Electric Vehicle (EV) and solar generation expansions?
e. How much of the proposed $6.8 billion T&D capital investment during 2023 - 2025 is to address EV and solar generation expansions?
f. Please identify and quantify how the $4.9 billion T&D invested during 2020 – 2022 reduced or will reduce operating or maintenance expenses. Provide the calculation in an unprotected spreadsheet.
g. Please identify and quantify how the proposed $6.8 billion T&D investment during 2023 - 2025 will reduce operating or maintenance expenses. Provide the calculation in an unprotected spreadsheet.
response:
No, without the Transmission & Distribution (“T&D”) investments proposed in the 2022 Rate Case, the Company does not believe it can continue to provide the same level of safe and reliable service that is enjoyed and expected by customers today. Continued investment in the T&D system, as proposed by the Company, is necessary to maintain a safe, reliable and resilient electric system, to accommodate the transition of the generation fleet, and to support the positive customer and economic growth that is currently taking place in the state.
For information on prior T&D investments, please refer to the testimony, discovery, and pleadings in Docket Nos. 36989 and 42516. For the planned T&D investments included/addressed in the 2022 Rate Case:
• Customer Growth and Economic Development: The Abramovitz-Adams-Houston-Robinson 2022 Rate Case testimony highlights that the Company has experienced positive year-over-year customer growth since 2012. Keeping in mind that Georgia was recently named the “Top State for Doing Business” for the eighth consecutive year by Area Development magazine, the reliability and dependability of the T&D system are increasingly important factors in facilitating economic development in the state. Given that state population trends and economic growth are expected to be above the national average in the coming years, robust system investment is required to continue attracting and serving new customers in Georgia.
• Grid Investment Plan: The increase in overall T&D capital spend directly correlates to the Company’s implementation of the Grid Investment Plan that was introduced in the Company's 2019 Base Rate Case proceeding. This plan comprises approximately 30% of the proposed T&D budget. The continued implementation of the Grid Investment Plan is necessary to improve reliability through investment in the worst performing feeders on the system along with the replacement of system assets that are approaching or have exceeded the end of their expected life. The Company anticipates that this investment will improve overall reliability and system resiliency and will reduce the frequency and duration of power outages experienced by customers and the transmission and distribution systems.
• Fleet Transition: Capital investment in the transmission system is also needed to support the transition of the Company’s generation fleet, which represents another factor driving T&D investments in the current case. As noted in the 2022 IRP, the retirement of various coal units and the continued addition	of renewable resources across the system requires transmission investment to facilitate the change in the Company’s resource mix. Transmission projects associated with unit retirement studies and strategic transmission projects associated with the Company’s North Georgia Reliability and Resilience Action Plan will commence within the 2023 – 2025 rate case window.
• Capital Maintenance: The replacement of deteriorating equipment also continues to be a priority for the Company. A significant portion of the Company’s T&D assets are approaching or have exceeded industry standards for expected life. Extensive investment in the system took place in the 1950’s and 1960’s to accommodate load growth that occurred in the state during that time. Though existing preventative maintenance practices have allowed the Company to extend the service lives of equipment well past their industry standard expected lives, the Company must continue to proactively identify equipment for replacement on a larger scale. Historic capital maintenance budgets have been funded at less than 1% of the asset population. This is not sustainable; therefore, more investment is required to prevent increased equipment failures and high replacement costs.
• Required System Projects: The Company will continue its commitment to working with federal, state, and local entities to perform various projects that are required for the benefit of customers and the general public. Examples include pole or structure relocations in support of state and local Department of Transportation (“DOT”) projects, make-ready projects to facilitate communication or governmental third-party pole attachments, substation physical security expenditures, replacement of failed transformers, and required system improvements resulting from projects performed by other ITS participants.
• Improvement of System Reliability: The Company consistently evaluates ways to improve and enhance the reliability of its transmission and distribution systems.  Reliability of the electric system remains an important factor in maintaining positive customer growth and ensuring that Georgia remains a great place to do business. With a sharp increase in work from home trends and increasing societal dependence on the grid (such as anticipated growth in the popularity of electric vehicles), the Company expects customers to have greater reliability expectations in the coming years.  Continued investment in projects such as the replacement of obsolete equipment, the deployment of equipment to enhance condition-based maintenance, installation of self-healing distribution networks, and the modernization of protective relays will support the enhancement of system reliability in the coming years.
The Company must consider the safety of the general public and Company employees, along with the reliability of the electric system, when making capital investment decisions. “Direct safety issues” and “reliability issues” are interrelated concepts, and it is not possible to identify projects that only “address direct safety issues” as opposed to “reliability issues.”  With this context in mind, most, if not all, of the capital T&D investments for 2020 – 2022 have positive impacts on the safety of the general public and the safety of the Company’s employees.
As referenced in subpart (b) above, most, if not all, of the proposed capital T&D investment for 2023 – 2025 have positive impacts on the safety of the general public and the safety of the Company’s employees.
Please note: Consistent with most load additions for customers, distribution upgrades that occur as a result of EV expansion projects are tracked as New Business projects and do not have a separate line item within the budget. Therefore, they are not captured in the numbers in the above table. Additionally, community charging EV facility work is not captured in the T&D budget.

Therefore, they are not captured in the numbers in the above table. Additionally, dollars associated with community charging EV facility work is not captured in the T&D budget. Lastly, dollars associated with unanticipated system improvements for Qualifying Facilities (QFs) or projects required for designation of third-party resources (such as Electric Municipalities) are not captured in the T&D budget.
The Company’s primary objective in making T&D investments is to continue providing safe, reliable, and resilient electric service to meet the needs of the Company’s customers. Operations and Maintenance (“O&M”) expense reductions are not the primary driver behind T&D capital investments for 2020 – 2022 or 2023 – 2025. Capital Maintenance investment:  The Company has increased its planned spend in some of the distribution asset management programs, including:
Emergency Pole Replacements and Damage
Defective Pole Replacement and Reinforcement
Storm Repairs
Underground Line Improvement or Replacement
Network Underground System Improvements
Failure to make these capital investments would risk (i) decreasing the speed and effectiveness of the Company’s storm response efforts, (ii) increased distribution pole failures, and (iii) increased in-service failures and unplanned outages on the underground network system.
Growth/Load Flow investment: Customer growth, economic development and fleet transition, as outlined in the Company’s response to STF-PIA-3-3 part (a), require addition; transmission Growth/Load Flow projects, which in turn, require additional distribution work. Distribution New Business Services
Distribution Transformers – New Business and Replacement
New Business Meters
Electric Vehicle Infrastructure investment through the Make-Ready program
Advanced Metering Infrastructure (“AMI”) Network Upgrades
Failure to make these capital investments risks the potential loss of positive customer growth, decreased system reliability, impaired growth and development of electric transportation in Georgia, and decreased network coverage for AMIs. Reliability investment: The Company has increased planned investments for projects that maintain and enhance system reliability. Specific projects include:
Condition Based Maintenance (CBM) deployment
Substation Integration Automation (SIA) projects
Relay Modernization projects
Failure to make these capital investments risks increased substation equipment failures, which negatively impacts safety and reliability, and decreased visibility on the condition of substation equipment.

115-kV transmission line facility rating remediation projects associated with the FAC-008 NERC reliability standard

Grid Investment: The Company has increased its planned investment in transmission projects that are included as part of the Grid Investment Plan. Specific items in this investment category include:
Union metal structures exceeding their expected life, thus requiring replacement of these structures
Using aging relays instead of aging regulators as part of the transmission criteria for inclusion in the Grid Investment Plan

question:

Georgia customer growth over the last 10 years 2012-2021

Georgia ‘economic growth’ over the last 10 years 2012-2021
Georgia Power ‘economic growth’ over the last 10 years 2012-2021
Georgia and US population trends over the last 10 years 2012-2021
response:
a. The growth in Georgia’s residential electric customers over the most recent 10 years of available data from Energy Information Administration (“EIA”), 2011-2020, was nearly 11%.
b. Residential customer growth in Georgia Power’s service territory has grown by 14% over the 2012-2021 period.
c. When discussing economic growth, economists tend to look at either Gross Domestic Product (“GDP”) at the U.S. level (Gross State Product (“GSP”) at the state level) or total non-agricultural employment. The Bureau of Economic Analysis (“BEA”) data shows Georgia’s Real (i.e., inflation adjusted) GSP, a measurement of the state’s economic output, grew by 28.6% over the last ten years from 2012 to 2021 (one of the top 10 states in the country). The BEA data indicates U.S. Real GDP grew by 22.2% during the same period. Georgia’s total non-agricultural employment grew by 761,900, or 19.5%, in the last 10 years (2012-2021), outpacing U.S. non- agricultural employment growth of 12.3%. On an annual average basis, Georgia had the 4th highest growth in non- agricultural employment in the country between 2012-2021.
d. There is no measure of Georgia Power economic growth. The Company operates in 155 of Georgia’s 159 counties, and therefore, its gross product or employment growth, as discussed in the response to subpart (c) above, would mimic the state’s growth in output and employment.
e. With respect to population growth, Georgia is one of the fastest growing states in the country, adding 988,000 new residents in the last 10 years (2011-2021), which represents the fourth highest population growth in the country. Georgia’s population grew by 10.1% from 2012-2021, outpacing U.S. population growth of 6.3% over this same period.

question:
The Company proposes to add “This customer generation must also have a local communications interface, installed, and maintained by the customer, that supports information exchange with, and control by, the Company.”
What information exchange and control capabilities would the Company require from customer generators under these rules? Would these capabilities follow any standard or protocol? If so, please describe
Why does the Company believe it should have control and information exchange with customer generation?
Is this proposed requirement related to the Company’s request for a DERMS?
Would this requirement be for all customer generators, or after a certain date?
response:
Please see Sections A13.1 through A13.3 in STF-PIA-6-40 Attachment.
The Company requires control and information exchange with a customer generation facility to adequately plan and operate the electric system in a safe, reliable, and efficient manner. From a planning perspective, a facility that peak-shaves or exports power to the Company’s electric system can mask the total amount of gross load the Company should plan to serve if the generation is not going to be available. Knowledge of how much power the facility will produce is especially critical during hot summer afternoons or cold winter mornings. Unavailability of the facility during these times could lead to thermal constraints on the electric system and possible loss of electric service to customers if the constrained element fails. Additionally, the ability of the Company to control (i.e., initiate changes in) how a facility exchanges real and reactive power with the Company’s electric system supports the efficient operation of the electric system and proper system voltage regulation, especially during times of high generation and low load.
From a safety perspective, a facility that operates in parallel with the Company’s electric system is capable of supplying currents to faults/short circuits on the system. Even though the Company requires facilities to have intertie protection and control devices to detect and initiate clearing of Company electric system faults via the facility interconnection breaker, the Company’s ability to remotely: (i) verify these settings are current, (ii) check the health of the facility interconnection breaker trip coil, and (iii) initiate opening of the facility interconnection breaker  will help ensure the safety of the general public and Company line crews that perform live-line work.
It is important to note that these requirements are defined by IEEE 1547-2018, IEEE Standard for Interconnection and Interoperability of Distributed Energy Resources and Associated Electric Power Systems Interfaces.
Yes. This requirement will help to ensure the success of the Company’s proposed DERMS.
With the exception of end-use customer-owned emergency or standby generators that create momentary parallel operation with the Company’s electric system, this proposed requirement is for all customer generators on the Company’s system (past, present, and future), sized 250 kW AC and above.
confidential_files: STF-PIA-6-54 Trade Secret Assertion.DOCX

The applicability section of the FPA tariff states that “FPA will be offered periodically, as determined by the Company, to eligible customers.”
In determining whether to make FPA offers, the Company considers uncertainties that could impact the projected inputs used in the development of the customer-specific off-peak price. Examples of these uncertainties include, but are not limited to, the uncertainty around environmental regulation or fuel markets that could impact the forecasted prices used in the development of FPA offers. In addition, uncertainty regarding historical customer loads, where used as a representation of typical customer operations, could impact the development of FPA offers.
