question: Please provide any and all studies, workpapers and supporting documents which the Company has performed or had performed on its behalf to support the conclusion that the Company’s modern rate designs (TOU-RD, TOU-PEV, TOU-REO) optimally reflect Georgia Power’s cost of service and will result in customers shifting electricity usage to benefit the customers.
response:
The Company did not assert in its testimony that its rates optimally reflect Georgia Power’s cost of service. Rather, Witness Legg states in his testimony that moving toward more modern rate structures and away from antiquated volumetric rate designs, such as the Residential Service (“R”) tariff, results in price signals that more appropriately reflect the cost of service. The Company’s residential time of use (“TOU”) rate options all provide a higher price signal during the on-peak hours of 2:00 – 7:00 pm on weekdays in the summer months of June through September (excluding holidays). These hours capture the periods when Georgia Power experiences its system peak loads, which results in these periods being the highest cost hours of the year. Conversely, the Company’s Time of Use - Plug-in Electric Vehicle (“TOU-PEV”) rate provides a super off-peak period with the price signal designed to encourage customers to charge their electric vehicle overnight when the system demands are much less and the cost to provide electricity is lower. As part of the rate design process, the Company reviews marginal costs by time period as another validation to the price signals being sent during the on and off-peak periods. Please refer to STF-PIA-6-55 Attachment for the results of the most recent analysis that was conducted in the Company’s PRICEM® model.
Overall, price signals to customers communicate how their behavior can impact their individual bill while also providing the opportunity to reduce costs to all customers and the Company over time. Industry best practice is to provide a significant price differential between the on-peak to off-peak periods, which all of the Company’s time of use rate designs accomplish, to encourage a behavioral change.
The design of the Time of Use – Residential Demand (“TOU-RD”) rate provides an even more efficient price signal as it is the only residential tariff that contains a price for demand-related costs. Demand-related costs are a known and proven cost-to-serve classification as documented in the NARUC Electric Utility Cost Allocation Manual and included in Georgia Power’s cost of service study. In fact, the majority of the non-fuel costs to serve residential customers are demand-related costs as shown in the Company’s Period I cost of service study filed in this case. By including the demand charge in the TOU-RD rate, customers receive a transparent price signal for the demand they place on the system.
The Company previously provided analysis and studies of customers’ behavior when participating on residential time of use rate options in response to STF-PIA-4-13 in Docket 42516. The Company has not conducted additional studies since the 2019 Base Rate case.
The Company’s time of use residential rate options are more modern in their design and send more appropriate price signals than the legacy Residential Service rate. Customers on time of use rates have the ability to shift their usage patterns from more expensive on-peak hours to less expensive off-peak hours in order to manage their energy costs. Customers on the TOU-RD rate have the additional option to save on electricity costs by managing their demand through the avoidance of simultaneous use of major appliances, which can be accomplished manually or through the use of smart appliances and technology. These price signals and opportunities to control electricity costs are in addition to the only savings option available to customers on Residential Service, which is to conserve or reduce total energy usage in order to save on their bill.

question: Please explain in detail how the design of the ECCR rider, as a percent of base bills excluding RTP incremental usage revenue, appropriately reflects cost causation associated with the Company’s coal combustion residual (“CCR”) compliance costs. Explain which portion of those costs, if any, is customer-related, demand-related, and energy-related.
response:
The ECCR rider applies as a percentage adder to all base revenues, which results in each component of a customer’s base tariff (basic service charge, energy charges, and demand charges) receiving an equal percentage adjustment to collect environmental compliance costs – including the CCR compliance costs. The collection of CCR compliance costs through the ECCR rider has been applied based on the Commission’s decision in the 2019 base rate case.
Generally, CCR compliance costs are demand-related costs. While the Company recognizes costs in categories of customer-related, demand-related, and energy-related in the Cost of Service study, its base rates collect for these costs using various structures. Some rates have specific basic service charges, energy charges, and demand charges while others may only include basic service charges and energy charges, and still other rates may have implicit demand charges within the energy pricing structure. By collecting the CCR compliance costs through the ECCR rate, the Company will continue to collect customer-related, demand-related, and energy-related costs in the same manner as it does with the existing base rate structures.

question:
Please refer to Evans Direct Testimony at Page 12 lines 9-13 stating “The MDS analysis utilized in this case is consistent with the those used in prior rate cases. The Company continually makes updates and refinements to its analyses to provide this Commission with the best information to make decisions and has continued to do so in this filing. The net result of these updates and refinements is a decrease to the percentage of customer-related costs resulting from the MDS analysis.”
Please provide the Company’s MDS analysis from its 2019 rate case and all associated workpapers in executable Excel spreadsheet form with all formulas and file linkages intact and all assumptions documented.
Please provide a comprehensive, detailed explanation of all “updates and refinements” made to the current MDS analysis from the analysis presented in the Company’s 2019 rate case.
Please describe the specific reasons and drivers of the stated “decrease to the percentage of customer-related costs resulting from the MDS analysis.”
response:
a. Please refer to STF-PIA-8-9 Attachment, which was previously provided in the Company’s response to STF-DEA-1-26 in Docket No. 42516.
b. In Account 364, the costs associated with Trusses were allocated with pole costs as opposed to towers and foundations. Similarly, the costs of pole caps were allocated with Poles rather than Fixture sets. The primary secondary split for poles is now based on pole height rather than conductor costs.
In Account 365, the allocation of “Other Unitized Equipment” which includes Switches, Repeaters, Reclosers, Sectionalizers, Protective Relays, Sensoring Equipment was modified to be based off the customer demand split from “Primary Lines” rather than allocated as 100% customer related.
In Account 367, the “Neutral Lines” costs allocation is based on the customer demand split for all lines not just secondary lines. The costs associated with pedestals were allocated with secondary costs rather than unlevelized costs. The calculation of the total feet of underground minimum system lines is based on the total line miles of underground cable multiplied by two.
In Account 368, the Regulator Bypass Switches were moved to be allocated with the Regulators, Capacitors, Auto-Boosters, and Reactors category. The zero-intercept for the overhead three-phase transformers based on single phase cost estimates was multiplied by three to reflect that three-phase transformers require three individual single-phase cans. The costs associated with three-phase transformer pads were separated from “Other Pad Related” costs and allocated based on the three-phase transformer split. The vintage adjustment to booked costs for Account 368 were determined by Georgia Power specific estimates for all booked equipment rather than South Atlantic region Handy Whitman Indices.
c. Updated cost estimates for poles and conductor yielded a smaller customer related cost component for Account 364 and Account 365, respectively. Allocating “Other Unitized Equipment” according to the “Primary Line” split as discussed in part ‘b’ above decreased the customer related costs for account 365. The Georgia Power specific vintage adjustment for booked costs in account 368 as discussed in part ‘b’ above decreased the customer related cost split for that account. The net result of updates and refinements is a decrease of customer-related costs resulting from the MDS analysis from 46.9% in 2019 to 32.6% in 2022.

question: Please identify any ratepayer benefit from the large “Customer Accounting” increase from $154 million in 2021 to approximately $194 million each year during 2023 – 2025.
response:
Please see the Company’s response to STF-PIA-9-3 for the drivers for the increase in Customer Accounting expenses for 2023 through 2025. The most significant driver is the implementation of the Customer Information System (CIS), which will replace the Company’s current customer service and billing system that has been in place since 1998. The Company continues to recognize the importance of investing in technology, applications, and equipment that allow it to provide the level of customer service its customers expect and deserve.  When selecting the appropriate technology, the Company focuses on enhancing the customer experience, employee efficiency, and costs to maintain the technology. CIS will allow Georgia Power to enhance its customers’ experience by improving its ability to manage customer information and requests, thereby providing more efficient customer service and more tailored solutions to meet customers’ needs. CIS will also integrate customer information into a single platform that enables customer service employees to quickly access customer information, thereby allowing them to provide customers with more comprehensive and timely solutions. Expected benefits include the ability to use data and automation to improve business outcomes and provide the needed flexibility in a changing industry which will provide further customer insights and information that will help customers better understand and manage their energy usage.
Another significant driver is the increase in customer payment transaction fees, which is the result of providing customers with multiple payment options and the increasing number of customers who choose to utilize these options.  These options are being increased to include other forms of payment such as digital wallet (PayPal, Venmo, Amazon Pay, Apple Pay, Google Pay) and payment card autopay, which will provide flexibility for customers and facilitate the payment process based on their choosing. Other drivers in this functional expense category are primarily related to general cost increases, including incremental inflation, the Company is experiencing in its existing business operations that is critical to providing safe and reliable service to its customers.

question: Please provide economic or cost benefit analysis to support the large increase in “Customer Accounting” expense during 2023 – 2025.
response: Please see the Company’s response to STF-PIA-9-3 for the drivers for the increase in Customer Accounting expenses for 2023 through 2025.  The Company has delayed the implementation of a new CIS system for as long as possible but Georgia Power, along with other Southern Company electric operating companies, are the last major utilities utilizing the current platform and it is becoming increasingly challenging to support as the resources available to support the current system are diminishing.  Therefore, a formal “cost benefit analysis” was not performed since keeping or updating the current system was not an option. All available replacement alternatives were considered and the vendor that best fit the requirements and was the most cost effective was selected. The increase in customer payment transaction fees was the result of providing customers with the flexibility of payment options which will facilitate the payment process for their benefit. The other cost increases are primarily related to general cost increases, including incremental inflation, that are necessary for the Company to provide service to its customers. Therefore, there are no economic or cost benefit analyses that were performed for these cost increases.

question: What percentage of customers currently on Flat Bill would be eligible for Budget Billing? Please describe in detail how this percentage was determined.
response:
Of all customer accounts currently on FlatBill, 58.7% are eligible for Budget Billing (58.5% of residential customers on FlatBill and 69.8% of non-residential customers on FlatBill).
There are four criteria an account must meet to be eligible for Budget Billing:
There must be 12 months of valid history billed to the customer at the premises
The account’s internal credit rating is A or B
The premises is limited to four or fewer individually metered active electric service points
The maximum monthly Budget Billing amount is less than $5,000
No customers on FlatBill were ineligible for Budget Billing under the third and fourth points.
To determine the percentage of customers on FlatBill eligible for Budget Billing, all accounts on FlatBill were evaluated to determine if they had at least 12 full months billed at the premises and an internal credit rating of A or B. Of the customers on FlatBill that are ineligible for Budget Billing, 75% are ineligible solely due to the internal credit rating, 18% are ineligible only because they lacked 12 full billing months at the premise, and 7% are ineligible for both reasons.

question: How is the Company planning on addressing demand charges at public DCFC chargers and at electrified fleet locations?
response: The Company has several rate options available to customers interested in installing electric vehicle chargers for public direct current fast charging or electrified fleet locations. In addition to the options that exist today, the Company has proposed the Charge It rider (CIEV-1) that pairs with Power and Light base tariffs. The CIEV-1 has a billing demand adjustment factor that reduces the billing demand on a Power and Light rate by 80% in the first year, 60% in the second year, 40% in the third year, and 20% in the fourth year. This temporary reduction to billing demands for new EV charging loads addresses the impact of demand charges as EV sales, and the additional charging loads that follow, increase in Georgia over the next few years. If approved, CIEV-1 would be exclusively available to new electric vehicle charging loads and will add to the Company’s existing portfolio of options to meet customers’ needs.

question: How does the Knowledge Base system handle synonyms and related terms in queries?
response:
The system dictionary uses concepts and synonyms to associate different words that have the same meaning with one another. A concept is simply a word and its synonyms, which the dictionary treats as a single object.
Intelligent Search uses concepts to match words in both users’ questions and in the Knowledge Base content, based on their meaning. It also recognizes that some concepts are more important to users than others and uses that information to prioritize answers within search results.

question: Please describe the process of updating and maintaining the Knowledge Base system.
response:
Oracle Knowledge Advanced (OKA) was configured to include several console level roles. These include KB_Author, KB_Reviewer/Approver, and KB_Manager. These roles must be requested from the Southern Company CoolCompliance. Requests must be reviewed and approved by an application owner and the employee’s manager.
Once approved, the user is provided access to the OKA Console where they can review, respond to, and implement suggestions for changes from end users to existing content within published articles.
All changes to article content are subject to independent review and must be approved by a KB_Reviewer/Approver or KB_Manager before publishing. An audit history of changes is captured within the platform for comparison with the current version of published articles. The audit history captures Date and Time, User, Version, Action Taken, Workflow Used, and Comments. If needed, the author can perform a side-by-side comparison of two versions of the article and can roll back changes if needed.

question: How does the Knowledge Base system handle natural language queries?
response:
A “locale” designates a language as it is used in a specific region or by a specific population. In applications that support multiple locales, each supported locale has a corresponding interface.
A locale or language is assigned to a “collection” to determine the available interfaces. Collections can be assigned to locales to make them available to only one interface, assigned to languages to make them available to all interfaces based on that language, or assigned to “Auto” to make documents in the collection available to any interfaces based on the detected language.

question: In what format were Georgia Power Company’s customer service standards maintained prior to the adoption of Knowledge Base? Does the Company maintain a copy of its customer service standards that were used before Knowledge Base was implemented? If so, how far back in time are these customer service standards maintained?

Prior to implementation of Oracle Knowledge Advanced (OKA), Customer Service Standards were maintained in a knowledge base supplied by a third-party vendor, eGain Corporation. The eGain Knowledge Base was implemented in 2018. These articles are still accessible via the eGain Console.
Prior to that system, Customer Service Standards were viewed and maintained via a series of intranet web pages using a platform known as TeamSite. These pages have since been retired and are no longer accessible.

question:
Were any Marginally Priced tariffs not available or offered to eligible customers during any months between April 2021 and April 2023? If so, please:
Identify which tariffs were not available or offered,
Explain why each tariff was not available or offered, and
In the same format as the Company’s Attachment STF-PIA-16-4.xlsx in Docket No. 42516, provide a spreadsheet showing all months during which the associated tariff was not available or offered during this period.
response:
In 2021, the Company made Fixed Pricing Alternative (“FPA”) offers available for customers that met the following criteria:
Customers who received an FPA offer in 2020 and were still interested
Customers that transitioned from RTP/MLM to RTP/TOU-RN as a result of the 2019 Rate Case Order and had expressed interest in transitioning to FPA in 2020, but due to the tariff requirements, were unable to receive an FPA offer and were waiting until they could qualify in 2021
For all other customers, FPA was not available for offers in 2021 due to the uncertainty around environmental regulation and the potential impacts to forecasted prices used in the development of the customer-specific off-peak rate.  In addition, the uncertainty of 2020 customer loads that would be used in the development of the customer-specific off-peak rate may not reflect typical operations due to the unique impact from the COVID-19 pandemic.
FPA was also not available for offers in 2022 through April 2023 due to continued uncertainty around environmental regulation and potential impacts to forecasted prices used in the development of the customer-specific off-peak rate.
The months during which an associated tariff was not available or offered are listed in STF-PIA-16-2 Attachment.

question:
Did the off-peak rate for customers receiving service on the FPA and TOU-RN tariffs change during 2022?  If so, please describe what impact the change had on the off-peak rate, the frequency of the changes, and the justification and calculation for the change.
Provide a spreadsheet showing the original off-peak rate, the new off-peak rate, the date the off-peak rate was changed for FPA and TOU-RN customers, from January 1, 2020 through December 31, 2022.
response:
Price changes for FPA and TOU-RN generally occur in the same manner and frequency as all other base tariffs and are only updated when the Company implements a Commission-approved rate change. The customer-specific off-peak prices for participants on FPA and TOU-RN changed in January 2021 and January 2022 as a result of implementing the 2019 rate case order. These tariff changes were part of rate case compliance filings made on 10/01/2020 and 10/01/2021 and were subsequently approved by the Commission on 10/28/2020 and 12/03/2021, respectively.  The effective percentage change to the off-peak prices was approximately 3.8% for all participants on FPA and 2.7% for all participants on TOU-RN in 2021, and approximately 5.8% for all participants on FPA and 4.8% for all participants on TOU-RN in 2022.
Please see the table below for the exact percentage changes to the customer-specific off-peak prices for FPA and TOU-RN customers, which were implemented to comply with the Commission’s order in the 2019 rate case:
 | January 2021 | January 2022
FPA Off-Peak % Change | 3.8156% | 5.7862%
TOU-RN Off-Peak % Change | 2.7397% | 4.7909%

response:
Please see the Company’s response to STF-PIA-16-3 regarding the 2022 price change to the off-peak rate for FPA and TOU-RN customers.
The off-peak rate for participants on FPA and TOU-RN is a customer-specific price. question: STF-WG-9-4 row 14. Please explain why easements were not obtained prior to beginning construction.
response:
As mentioned in the Company’s response to STF-PIA-20-1 part (d) subpart (ii), it is important to note that variations can occur when transitioning from planning-grade scopes to engineering-grade scopes. The REDACTED transmission line was originally located on the road right-of-way. As part of the project design and the location process, the transmission line was shifted away from the road right-of-way due to conductor clearance requirements under wind-displaced conditions, thereby necessitating multiple easements.
It is important to note that the Company did acquire multiple easements prior to the start of construction.  However, acquiring an easement from one particular property owner proved to be very challenging, which caused delays to the project. The Company initially contacted this property owner in November 2021, with the presentation of a proposed easement beginning in February 2022. Construction on this project began in July of 2022. Despite continuous efforts to address the affected property owner’s concerns, challenges persisted throughout 2022 regarding the location of a transmission structure. The required easement was ultimately secured, and the project was completed in May 2023.

question:
Has the Company investigated the use of amorphous core transformers?
If so, please identify the pros and cons of amorphous core transformers in relation to standard transformers traditionally used by the Company.
If not, please explain.
response:
The Company currently has amorphous core transformers on its distribution system.
The pros and cons are as follows:
Pros:
Lower no-load (core) losses compared to silicon steel core transformers.
Cons:
Requires a larger transformer core and more windings, which leads to an increase in weight and dimension.
Larger dimensions could lead to larger required pads for pad-mounted designs.
Larger dimensions and increase in weight could lead to re-design of existing pole installations and require larger poles in new installations.
Transportation and material handling procedures and practices could change due to larger, heavier units.
The amorphous core material can be more expensive to produce than silicon steel cores.
Core noise is increased in comparison to a silicon steel core transformer.
Ferroresonance is more likely with a low-loss transformer.
There is mixed data on the short-circuit withstand of amorphous core transformers vs. silicon steel designs.

question: Please detail how the company will determine the relevant tariff for large-load customers, as well as how the new tariff will meet the revenue requirement attributable to serving large-load customers.
response:
The tariff revisions the Company filed with the Commission on February 28, 2025, collectively require new customers with an expected total peak demand of 100 MW or greater at one or more premises located on one tract or contiguous tracts of land to take service on the Time of Use Supplier Choice (TOU-SC) Monthly Access Charge (MAC) option.  MAC was approved in the 2022 base rate case, and multiple customers are either taking service or have contracted to take service on the rate.
Per the TOU-SC tariff, customers on the MAC option pay a customer-specific Monthly Access Charge. All energy is billed at the hourly Real Time Pricing – Day Ahead price effective for that hour. The MAC is computed by the Company based on the cost to serve the customer’s load and location to meet the Company’s financial requirements.  Additionally, the minimum bill provisions in the Contract for Electric Service Addendum will serve as an additional assurance that expected base revenue will at a minimum recover the incremental expected annual base revenue requirements.

question: For large storm events such as Hurricane Helene, indicate if the Company has one or more target metrics or quantitative goals for outage restoration times that is factored directly or indirectly into the number and type of resources acquired and/or the various storm response logistics modeling tools.  If so, identify and describe each such target metric or quantitative goal and describe the manner in which it is used to determine the number and type of resources acquired, including, but not limited to, the various storm response logistics modeling tools.
response:
The Company does not have specific metrics or quantitative goals for outage restoration times that factor into the number and type of resources needed for initial preparations of the storm response. Once the initial storm event has occurred and damage for various areas has been assessed by the Company, it assigns an outage event level from 1 through 4, which can be used as an input for resourcing decisions.  The outage event level also helps determine an Estimated Restoration Time (ERT) to track restoration times for customers. ERTs are developed and communicated for major storms using a cross-functional team as mentioned in the Company’s response to STF-PIA-29-1.
At the onset of significant outage events, it is difficult to accurately determine the extent of electrical system damage due to continuing extreme weather conditions, darkness, or incomplete damage assessment. The Company has established the four outage event level definitions to provide consistent guidance for restoration management and communication to its customers. These guidelines provide expectations around when customers should receive an ERT and how ERTs are managed. The Company does not wait for a complete damage assessment before exercising the event level guidelines; rather, an initial decision of storm level is made early in a major event prior to finishing a complete assessment of the electric system.

question: Provide a copy of all internal or external reviews or critiques, including lessons learned, prepared by or for the Company or by a reviewing entity of the Company’s performance in its response to Hurricane Helene.
response:
Following the Company’s response to Hurricane Helene, a cross functional team was brought together to review the Company’s storm response process. As a result of this qualitative review, the Company identified eight areas for assessment and, where appropriate, further action. The Company is currently addressing these areas and anticipates completion later in 2025.
Develop a base camp playbook for leaders to utilize to successfully run a base camp.
Update the Significant Event Level Estimated Restoration Time Management document to better accommodate needs for restoration events with a 1 to 2 week duration.
Determine a process for assigning storm roles to every new and existing employee at the Company and providing necessary training for the newly assigned roles.
Develop a process for hosting an annual Company-wide storm drill and include a scenario of a severe hurricane impacting the whole state, including Metro Atlanta, in the first drill.
Standardize the Company’s approach to local (county/city) communication during major storm events.
Evaluate and update the safety onboarding process for off-system personnel.
Develop a standardized process for damage assessment data collection and delivery.
Refresh storm preparedness checklists included in all region Storm Emergency Response Plans.

response: There are no specific metrics or documented goals for Hurricane Helene restoration efforts; however, the primary aim during any storm event is to safely and efficiently restore electric service to all affected customers as quickly as possible. This includes prioritizing public safety, critical infrastructure (such as hospitals and emergency services), and effective communication with the public. The process involves assessing storm damage, mobilizing and deploying repair crews and resources, coordinating with local agencies, and providing timely updates to customers throughout the restoration process. question:
Describe the manner in which the Company recorded the Hurricane Helene capital costs for accounting purposes and provide a copy of all documentation relied on for this purpose, whether GAAP, USOA, other authoritative sources, and/or all internal guidelines and/or procedures.

Confirm that only costs that did not qualify for capitalization were recorded to the storm reserve.
response:
The Company follows the requirements set forth in U.S. GAAP regarding capitalization of Property, Plant, and Equipment costs. ASC 360-05-3 indicates that “Property, plant, and equipment typically consist of long-lived tangible assets used to create and distribute an entity's products and services and include: (a) Land and land improvements, (b) Buildings, (c) Machinery and equipment, (d) Furniture and fixtures.” Additionally, Accounting Standards Codification 360-30-1 states “the historical cost of acquiring an asset includes the costs necessarily incurred to bring it to the condition and location necessary for its intended use.
During a storm response, all costs except base O&M expenses and capital plant assets associated with meters and transformers are recorded to the storm regulatory asset.  The remaining Distribution and Transmission capital costs initially recorded to the storm regulatory asset are later identified and transferred from the storm regulatory asset to the appropriate capital plant asset accounts following the storm based on the requirements stated above. Therefore, capital costs are excluded and only the incremental storm costs that do not qualify for capitalization are included in the storm regulatory asset.

question: For Hurricane Helene, provide all documents related to any analysis performed by, on behalf of, or at the direction of the Company that identifies the amount of mobilization or demobilization time billed, and the amount of mobilization or demobilization time paid, and that supports the reasonableness of these hours and costs incurred to respond to the storm and/or the related restoration work for which cost recovery will be requested.
response:
The Company’s efforts related to mobilization or demobilization for its own employees related to storms follow its normal internal approval process for timesheets. This process requires review and approval of both time submitted and appropriate account coding.
The Company’s contracts with third parties are structured on an hourly basis for both labor and equipment and, in general, follow an industry standard process for mobilization and demobilization.  This process consists of working with the vendor(s) to understand the Company’s needs and expectations, often days in advance of the storm, that eventually leads to establishing an expected time for their departure from the vendor’s home base work location to be available at the Company’s specified location and time.  Billing begins when the contractors initially arrive at their respective departure location (i.e., vendor home base work location). Once the contractors have arrived at the designated work location, their typical work hours during storm restoration consist of 16 hours per day, which is consistent with industry standards. Work includes all work activities the Company directs, including, but not limited to, travel time to and from damaged areas, safety briefings, meals, damage assessment time, and standby time, as necessary and prudent. During storm restoration efforts, the vendor submits daily timesheets for time and equipment which are reviewed for reasonableness for total time worked with stated equipment but is not segregated by specific work activity.
For demobilization, the Company works with the vendor to initiate the demobilization process to understand and establish expectations that leads to a mutual understanding of the expected time of their departure from the Company’s specified work location back to the vendor’s home base work location, at which time, billing ends. Updates and ongoing communication occur as necessary when and if travel time would not match reasonable expectations, including instances where a vendor may be redeployed for storm restoration work for another utility. Based on the contractors’ origination, the criteria referenced above, and continual conversations, the Company develops a reasonable understanding of the time required for mobilization and demobilization.

response:
The Company utilizes software and program tools designed to identify discrepancies in billing. These tools generate alerts that create billing exceptions whenever bills deviate from the expected parameters or are not processed correctly.
App changes include the following testing processes, listed in sequential order:
Manual functional testing, where a human tester acts as an end-user to compare actual results to expected outcomes.
Automated regression testing, a software testing method that automatically re-runs a set of old tests on a software application after a code change to ensure that existing features are unimpacted by the code change.
Smoke testing by internal users, which involves internal users running high-level tests to ensure the most important critical path features are functional in a production environment.

question:

response:

question: Was any pilot or demonstration project conducted before selecting SwissDrones? If so, please provide results, findings, and lessons learned.

These evaluations were conducted in October 2022 and February 2023 and provided the FAA with direct performance and safety data from the SwissDrones platform. The results supported the FAA’s determination that the aircraft was appropriate for commercial BVLOS operations in support of utility infrastructure.
Purchase of the system did not occur until after the FAA had formally reviewed and approved the aircraft for this use case. This ensured Southern Company only invested in a platform with a federally validated safety case.
In addition, the SwissDrones SDO 50 had previously undergone extensive evaluation as part of the Xcel Energy BVLOS Capital Project, one of the earliest federally recognized initiatives to test long-range BVLOS inspection concepts. Lessons learned from that national program—including endurance, detect-and-avoid strategies, and corridor patrol efficiencies—directly informed Southern Company’s approach.

question: Has Georgia Power, Southern Company or any other entity on behalf of the Company or Southern Company, determined that the SwissDrones platform will be cost effective and the best choice for transmission line inspection? If so, please provide. If not, please explain.

This visibility with the FAA is important for securing future approvals that could enable even greater cost savings and inspection efficiencies across the system.

question: What role does DSM play in informing rate design at GPC?

For example, time-of-use rates encourage customers to use energy during off-peak times, demand charges encourage managing peak usage, and hours use demand rates encourage higher load factors.

question: Is there a benchmark mechanism to determine the success of a tariff?

question: Please share what customer surveys GPC has performed in the past 3 years. Provide results as well as statistical analysis of the Customer Service Satisfaction surveys. If no surveys were performed, please explain.
response:
Georgia Power employs a multi-pronged approach to customer feedback, leveraging both industry-standard benchmarks from syndicated studies and internal survey tools to directly poll customers about their experiences and sentiment. Some of those surveys include those that measure customer satisfaction, loyalty, product satisfaction, channel satisfaction, and brand image.
For its customer satisfaction corporate goals, Georgia Power leverages the national J.D. Power Electric Utility Customer Satisfaction Index for residential and general business benchmarks and Net Promoter Score (“NPS”) loyalty surveys for large commercial & industrial customers with an assigned account manager.
J.D. Power Electric Utility Customer Satisfaction Study
Georgia Power subscribes to and is included in J.D. Power’s Electric Utility Customer Satisfaction Studies for both residential and business customers. These studies assess satisfaction across eight dimensions of Price/Cost, Safety & Reliability, Trust, Ease of Doing Business, Digital Channels, People, Problem Solving, and Information Provided (Communications).
Performance: Scores are reported on a 1,000-point scale and the results are included as a portion of the Company’s operational metrics. See the table below for 2022 through 2024 results. Through the first two quarters of 2025, Georgia Power continues to be ranked number one amongst peer utilities in the South in the J.D. Power residential and business studies.
J.D. Power Full Year Results
 | 2022 | 2023 | 2024
J.D. Power Electric Utility Residential Customer Satisfaction Index Score | 774 | 769 | 749
J.D. Power Index rank for Residential, South Large | 1st of 12 utilities | 1st of 12 | 1st of 12
J.D. Power Electric Utility Business Customer Satisfaction Index Score | 827 | 785 | 838
J.D. Power Index rank for Business, South Large | 1st of 11 utilities | 3rd of 11 | 1st of 11
Key Drivers: Energy prices have been the primary driver of J.D. Power index scores in the past couple of years and are especially applying downward pressure to residential results. Ease of Doing Business and Problem Resolution appeared as opportunities for improvement at mid-2024 as service-related opportunities, and the Company is addressing these areas for improvement. The industry as a whole has faced significant affordability challenges.
Managed Account Net Promoter Score® (MANPS) Surveys
Managed accounts are surveyed using the NPS methodology. This methodology measures loyalty by asking customers in this segment to imagine if they could choose their electric utility, how likely would they be to recommend Georgia Power to a friend or colleague, with a 0 being would not at all recommend to a 10 being would most definitely would recommend. Scores are determined by taking the percent of customers who gave a 9 or 10 rating and subtracting the percent of customers who provided a 0 – 6 rating and multiplying by 100. ((% 9s and 10s) - (% 6s and below)) x100. Ratings of a 7 and 8 are discarded.
Performance: NPS scores are tracked quarterly. See the table below for 2022 through 2024 results. Through the second quarter of 2025, Georgia Power’s score was 75 (scale of -100 to 100), which is considered outstanding based on marketing research standards applied across most industries.
 | 2022 | 2023 | 2024
MANPS | 64 | 68 | 67
Key Drivers: Consistently, Power Reliability and Account Manager Responsiveness are cited as top factors influencing positive ratings among promoters in the study. Electricity costs are named as a concern more often by the few detractors (ratings of 6 and below) the Company has seen over the past three years.
Other Surveys Conducted:
Customer Experience “Companion Surveys”
These internal surveys complement J.D. Power results and are used to assess overall satisfaction, trust, and ease of doing business, as well as including questions about certain experiential factors such as customer contact channels used, outages experienced, and communications awareness. They are administered quarterly for both residential and business customers.
Transactional Surveys
These are used for specific customer interactions to help understand the customer experience when engaging with Georgia Power. Transactional surveys are short, targeted surveys administered immediately after a customer interaction. They are designed to measure satisfaction with specific touchpoints such as agent-managed service calls, self-service IVR transactions, and digital engagement experiences. They include measures such as likelihood to recommend the transaction channel, satisfaction with the experience, and effort. Additional transactional surveys include those for Post-Grid Improvement (survey sent to customers impacted by the Grid Improvement Program), Georgia Power Land Right-of-Way (“ROW”) (survey where the Company has purchased land for ROW), Georgia Power Property Managers (survey of property managers’ experience with their portal).
Product Satisfaction Surveys
•	Georgia Power gathers customer feedback through surveys related to their enrollment and installation experiences across various regulated and unregulated programs and solutions. While many of these surveys are ongoing, some are conducted as one-time opportunities to gather targeted insights. The surveys are typically short and focus on satisfaction, experience, and NPS ratings. Some programs that are surveyed include: Solar Installation, Small Commercial Direct Install, EV Charger Rebate Program Participation, Electric Transportation Make Ready Program Participation, AllConnect, and Vivint.
Image and Brand
•	Image and brand surveys are conducted annually and include focus groups of 20-30 customers as well as a quantitative study of 2,000 customers to gauge customer sentiment and awareness around Georgia Power brand perception, customer needs, messaging impact, etc.

As a support function, the QA team evaluates calls according to the Key Performance Indicators (“KPIs”) defined by call center leadership. Please see STF-PIA-36-4 Attachment, which describes these KPIs.
Each evaluation form assigns point values to specific behaviors or metrics based on their impact on customer experience. During the review of customer interactions, the QA team not only listens to the conversation between the customer and the agent but also examines the customer’s account across various systems such as the Customer Service System, Service Cloud, Online Customer Care, and Workspaces. This ensures that the correct order, notation, and other applicable actions were taken on the customer’s behalf. Additionally, the QA team assesses whether the agent has provided the customer with complete and accurate information, as well as offered options that could benefit the customer and enhance their relationship with the Company as a trusted resource. Points are deducted for each evaluation behavior that does not meet current standards. For example, minor issues may result in a 1-point deduction, while more serious concerns could lead to a 10-point deduction or more. The findings are documented in a QA evaluation.
QA specialists assess each KPI during call reviews, deduct points as appropriate, and provide detailed written feedback. This feedback includes explanations for point deductions, recommended corrective actions, and links to relevant training materials or knowledge base articles. Once the evaluation form is submitted, a final score is calculated. For Georgia Power, the goal for QA scoring is 85% or greater.
At the end of each month, QA results are shared with call center leadership to provide insights into customer experience trends, overall performance, and potential disciplinary actions. QA also partners with the training team to identify opportunities for additional agent development. Throughout the month, if a QA specialist identifies any egregious behaviors during an evaluation, they immediately notify the agent’s supervisor so that prompt corrective action can be taken.

question:

response:
The Company does not currently have a mechanism in place to determine why a call is terminated by the phone system. However, the Company’s overflow process is the primary driver of call terminations by the system. During rare demand spikes (such as severe weather), the Company activates and maintains an overflow process using the Interactive Voice Response (“IVR”) system. When the IVR system is activated, the overflow menu provides a limited set of options, including the ability to report an outage. However, the IVR system does not include an option to speak directly to a live agent. Thus, customers who want to speak to an agent can choose to exit the menu by terminating the call and then call back.  While the number of call terminations are not tracked, the Company understands that this system is the most likely reason why a call would be terminated.

If large loads affect a GIP project, the Company may continue the original scope of the GIP project or cancel the GIP project and initiate a non-GIP project to accommodate any impacts from large load. This optimization process is coordinated through cross functional stakeholder meetings to align work scopes and ensure efficient execution.

question: Please provide the current formula and methods used to calculate Budget Billing amounts for new Budget Billing customers and for adjusting the Budget Bill of existing Budget Bill customers. In addition, please identify any changes to the formula and methods for calculating or recalculating Budget Bills over the past 5 years. Additionally, provide factors that would require a budget bill to be recalculated mid-cycle or earlier than originally scheduled. When would this be triggered in the current formulas?
response:
Method for calculating Budget Billing amount for new customers
The initial Budget Billing calculation for new customers (customers are eligible if they have at least 12 months of billing history and meet certain credit rating requirements) is based on the sum of the most recent 12-month history of the Electric Service Bill for the premises divided by 12. The last 12 months of billing history includes all billing components: basic service charge, base rate, fuel, riders, and taxes, as well as additional electric service at the premise: metered, un-metered, and electric lighting.
There have not been any changes to this methodology in the past 5 years.
Budget Billing Monthly Review Calculation
As part of its review, the budget bill amount for every customer is recalculated monthly based on the average of the most recent 12-month history to analyze if the monthly bill amount needs to be adjusted. The analysis includes any over or under collection on the account from the previous months.
If the new budget bill amount differs by more than $5.00 and 10% of the current budget bill amount, this new amount will be effective with next month’s bill. At the anniversary date of inception, the new budget bill amount will be effective regardless of whether it exceeds the threshold for re-establishing the monthly bill amount.

question:
Please describe whether the June net rate decrease triggered any automatic adjustments to Budget Billing amounts. Please specify
whether automatic recalculation was performed,
the date on which such recalculation occurred (if applicable), and
the logic used to determine whether a recalculation was required.
response:
The June net rate decrease did not trigger any automatic adjustments to Budget Billing amounts.  A rate change of any type (base rate, fuel, other riders) is incorporated in the calculation of the deferred amount. Under Budget Billing, customers continue to pay their established budget amount, while the difference between the amount and the customer’s actual billed charges is accumulated in the deferred balance. When rates change, the customer’s actual billed charges are calculated using the new rates, which affects the amount recorded in the deferred balance. The deferred balance is then incorporated into future monthly Budget Billing recalculations that use the customer’s most recent 12-month history.
Please also see the Company’s response to STF-PIA-39-8 for a detailed explanation of the Budget Billing calculation.

question: Please describe any asset life extension program or conditioned-based line/component replacement program the Company has used to replace/reinforce vulnerable aging transmission and distribution lines and station components, thereby avoiding expensive complete replacements. Describe the software used to support the program and provide copies of any internal documents/reports/ guidelines.
response:
The fundamental objective of the Company’s maintenance program is to ensure that system equipment will perform reliably while it is providing service to customers. The Company’s preventative maintenance practices, many of which are outlined in its response to STF-WG-1-27, are intended to extend the life of system assets for as long as practical without jeopardizing reliability. Through robust and comprehensive maintenance work, the Company routinely extends the life of equipment beyond its industry expected life. For example, transformers and breakers that will be greater than 50 and 35 years old, respectively, by the end of the Grid Investment Plan period are eligible for replacement within the Grid Investment Plan. The industry expected life for transformers and breakers is 35 years and 25 years. While the Company takes great pride in its maintenance programs and its ability to extend the useful life of its assets, it also understands that neither preventative maintenance nor condition-based programs can avoid the need for eventual replacement of assets, as aged equipment beyond industry expected life must be contemplated for replacement due to increased risks of failures that would trigger costly emergency replacements and reduced reliability to customers.
The Company performs routine asset inspections that may inform decisions regarding component replacement, component repair, or asset replacement altogether. Various assessments are performed during these inspections to decide whether to repair or replace system equipment, including the age of the asset, the condition of the asset, the operational history of the asset, availability of vendor technical support for the asset, and the availability of spare parts and specialized testing/maintenance equipment for the asset. These assessments sometimes trigger asset component replacement instead of complete asset replacement.
Examples of transmission components that could be replaced due to condition include flashed insulator, degraded splices, broken ground conductor, transformer bushings, transformer seals (gaskets), transformer positive pressure systems (Nitrogen blankets), transformer conservator tank bladders, transformer de-energized tap changers, on-load tap changer  mechanisms and contacts, breaker interrupters or vacuum bottles, breaker interrupting medium (oil or SF6, based on condition testing), bad trip coils and heaters on breakers, updated breaker mechanism lube practices, rusted transformers, rusted structures, rusted overhead ground wire, and anchor/foundation repairs.
Examples of distribution components that could be replaced or reinforced due to condition include wood poles (either by treatment, reinforcement, woodpecker damage repair, or pole cap installation), rusted transformers, rusted structures, lightning arresters, and insulators.
The Company uses numerous tools to assist in the inspection, assessment, and maintenance of system assets. Some examples include:
Transmission Lines Maintenance System (TLMS): A software tool that is used to manage all inspection and repair work orders. It is used manage the Company’s abnormal situation (“ABSIT”) data from work order creation to completion.
Transmission Lines Inspection System (TLIS): An ARCGIS based field application that is used to conduct inspections. The application receives work orders from the TLMS application and upon field completion of the inspection, it returns asset data to Standard Transmission Operations and Maintenance Program application (“STOMP”) and abnormal situations identified to TLMS.
Standard Transmission Operation and Maintenance Program (STOMP): An asset management database and software used to track and maintain transmission equipment throughout its lifecycle. This database also feeds GIS and mapping systems for visualization of the Company’s system.
Southern Company Substation Maintenance Procedures: A set of matrices and procedures that define the maintenance cycles of substation equipment, based on classification and environmental operating conditions.
Doble Test Assistant Software (DTA): The DTA software is a data repository for current and historical substation power factor testing results. Trends or significant changes in test results are used to determine no action or possible transformer or equipment replacement.
Dissolved Gas Analysis (DGA) Test Lab Database: A database of primarily substation transformer dissolved gas analysis test results taken manually at specific intervals. Allows the ability to trend historical DGA data and make decisions on those trends.
eDNA/OSI-Soft Pi Analytic Software: Analytic data historian software that, both historically and currently, is utilized to receive and trend online DGA sampling for transformers. eDNA is the retiring system, and OSI-Soft Pi is its replacement.
Breaker Event File Collection & Analysis: A breaker operation analysis tool that allows the Company to review and trend real time operations of medium and high voltage breakers. The Company uses this analysis to trend important key operational functions and trigger maintenance response for results that are out of target.
Systems With Intelligence (SWI) Infrared monitoring: Online infrared monitoring of transformers that allows for continuous collection of transformer temperature readings and analysis.
Power Delivery Enterprise Asset Management (PDEAM): A combination of software and systems that is used to maintain the Company’s assets. This tool allows for enterprise integration with multiple systems, and it was developed to optimize the quality and utilization of assets throughout their lifecycle, increase productive uptime, and reduce operational costs. The tool also connects to the Company’s GIS asset database, which allows for the planning and tracking of maintenance on Company’s assets.
Fulcrum: Allows for bulk orders to be created and completed for specific broad reaching maintenance tasks which are then electronically shared with field personnel for completion. This tool also serves as a data storage point for maintenance activities completed within the program, which do not originally require engineering and individual work order creation. Fulcrum offers real time productivity tracking and reporting for individual field personnel and initiatives.

question:
Please refer to Docket No. 11941, Georgia Power Reliability and Quality of Electric Service Annual Filing.
Please provide an explanation of why system reliability has deteriorated as indicated with the major rise of SAIDI in 2019.
Year | 2014 | 2015 | 2016 | 2017 | 2018 | 2019 | 2020 | 2021
SAIDI | 102.76 | 114.92 | 111.06 | 116.42 | 125.2 | 147.75 | 142.22 | 141.13
SAIFI | 1.20 | 1.31 | 1.17 | 1.16 | 1.21 | 1.27 | 1.33 | 1.25
Why has SAIDI remained at that level for the years 2020 and 2021?
Does the Company still use the Worst Performing Circuit reliability improvement approach?
If so, how does it supplement/augment the Distribution Improvement Plan?
If not, what are the reasons and why was it replaced with the Distribution Improvement Plan?
Was vegetation management/improvement part of the Worst Performing Circuit approach?
After the rise in SAIDI in 2019 and remaining at that level for the years 2020 and 2021, what changes were made in the Worst Performing Circuit reliability improvement approach?
response:
There are many variables that impact Georgia Power’s SAIDI metric. Weather, vegetation, vehicle accidents, and equipment failure are the leading contributors to the Company’s SAIDI, with weather making the largest contribution. Significant variances in any of these drivers year to year can have a significant impact on SAIDI. Considering the impact of weather alone, National Weather Service reports indicate there were nearly three times as many tornados in Georgia in 2019 than in 2018. Furthermore, there was a 20% increase in the number of severe weather reports of any type in Georgia in 2020 over 2019. Such pronounced increase in severe weather is a significant driver of the change in SAIDI noted above.
While weather is a driver, it is not the only driver behind the change in performance beginning in 2019. When comparing the SAIDI results filed in Docket No. 11941 year over year, one must be aware that the methodology used to calculate SAIDI for this filing is the 2.5-Beta method outlined in IEEE 1366-2012. A weakness of the 2.5-Beta method is the influence that catastrophic events can have on a company’s results for five years after said event. A catastrophic event will raise the threshold for what is considered an excluded major event day, thereby characterizing more storm activity as “normal” and included in a company’s results. Since the 2.5-Beta method considers five years of history, the major event day threshold can remain elevated for five years and therefore mask a company’s true reliability performance during typical operating conditions.
Georgia experienced such a catastrophe in 2017 in the form of Hurricane Irma, which was a devastating storm that impacted much of the state. Hurricane Irma impacted the Company’s major event day threshold as described above. Since 2017 remains in the five-year calculation window for the 2.5-Beta method, the Company’s major event day threshold since 2017 has been roughly 25% higher than in the preceding four years. This has the effect of increasing the Company’s SAIDI performance because more disruptive events are considered normal than in years prior to 2018. To illustrate this effect, the table below lists what the Company’s SAIDI performance would have been from 2018 through 2021 had the Company’s major event day threshold remained constant since 2017.
Year | 2018 | 2019 | 2020 | 2021
SAIDI As Filed | 125.2 | 147.75 | 142.22 | 141.13
SAIDI w/ Constant Threshold | 125.15 | 131.22 | 135.27 | 133.5
Please see the response to part (a) above. Severe weather activity and the statistical artifact created by Hurricane Irma are primary drivers to SAIDI performance in 2020 and 2021 remaining consistent with 2019.
Yes, the Company still carries out a worst performing feeder program.
While the worst performing feeder program and the Grid Investment Plan have the common objective of identifying and addressing issues with feeders that exhibit poor reliability, the two programs are significantly different. The worst performing feeder program is notably smaller in scale compared to the Grid Investment Plan and makes limited investments to improve circuits that were among the worst performers in the prior 24 months. The Grid Investment Plan generally seeks to solve the root causes of outages on circuits that are consistently poor reliability performers – resulting in larger scale projects targeted to the causes of outages on each circuit. Due to these differences, the worst performing feeder program and the Grid Investment Plan have unique qualification criteria for feeders included in the plan and use different sets of solutions. Some circuits may be worked on under both initiatives with issues initially addressed by the targeted solutions of the worst performing feeder program and later addressed by full-scale solutions implemented under the Grid Investment Plan, with the aim of not returning to the circuit for additional work in the future.
See the Company’s response to part (c)(i) above.
Targeted vegetation management is sometimes employed on worst performing feeder projects. The Company often finds that problematic vegetation conditions exist outside its rights-of-way. In such cases, it is not uncommon for other solutions to be required in order to reduce customer exposure to resulting faults.
Prior to 2019, investments made in worst performing feeder program circuits did not fully remediate reliability issues on circuits in their entirety. The approach was to deploy finite funding amounts towards incremental improvement on a greater number of feeders rather than target a larger improvement on a small number of feeders. Since 2019, the Company has employed a feeder segmentation strategy in its worst performing feeder program. The current practice is to deploy enough intelligent line devices to divide a worst performing feeder into segments of 300 to 500 customer. Using this strategy reduces the number of customers that are impacted by a given fault on the distribution feeder. This strategy further takes advantage of the Company’s fault location, isolation, and service restoration capabilities first deployed in the early 2010s.

Present-day maximum loading, expected load growth, and any other factors which might add to future line loading over and above the forecasted level. For example, an area where numerous solar facilities have been built might be expected to attract further solar development, thereby biasing the decision to a higher-capacity conductor than would otherwise be considered.
The condition, height, and strength of the line’s structures and the terrain that the line crosses.
A few standard sizes are favored to keep down the costs of stocking conductors, connectors, and tools needed to make repairs.
The concerns of and input from maintenance personnel are also considered. For example, in certain conductor types, if a break occurs under tension, the core can withdraw away from the break and require longer amounts of conductor to be replaced.
A good balance between cost and capacity is generally sought when selecting conductors for transmission line projects.

question: Describe the Company’s calculation of the standard cost for capital (plant) items recorded to plant accounts in the normal course of business. Describe each component, including, but not limited to, inventory cost, payroll and related costs loads, supervision and engineering loads, A&G expense loads, thirty party contractor loads, and other loads. Describe how each component is calculated, including the source data, the calculations underlying each percentage load, and the base against which the load is applied. The response also should differentiate between distribution capital items; transmission capital items; specific capital items, such as meters and transformers; and other functional and/or other capital items to the extent there are any differences. Provide a copy of all accounting guidelines and/or procedures that describe these calculations.
response:
The Company includes both direct and indirect costs in the cost for capital projects as described in the Company’s General Accounting Procedures (GAP) 55, provided in STF-SCR-2-11 Attachment. Direct costs are those costs directly charged to a project, including labor and materials. The Company allocates indirect overhead construction costs to capital projects in compliance with the FERC Code of Federal Regulations (“CFR”) Title 18, Part 101, Electric Plant Instructions Section 4. This allows for the capitalization of “all overhead construction costs, such as engineering, supervision, general office salaries and expenses, construction engineering and supervision by others than the accounting utility, law expenses, insurance, injuries and damages, relief and pensions, taxes and interest”. The methodologies to capture and allocate these costs are described below.
The ad valorem allocation is applicable to distribution and transmission projects.  This allocation records property tax expense for open capital projects that have incurred charges as of December of the prior year. The base is equal to the prior December Construction Work in Progress (“CWIP”) balance and a composite millage rate, based on the prior year’s actual millage rates, is applied to the base.  This allocation debits FERC Account 107, Construction work in progress and credits FERC Account 408, Taxes other than income taxes.
The Engineering and Supervision (“E&S”) and Administrative and General (“A&G”) allocations, including Shared Services, are applicable to distribution and transmission projects. E&S allocations are used to accumulate costs associated with construction related engineering and supervisory activities that support multiple capital projects and cannot be directly assigned to a specific project.  The A&G allocation is used to allocate overhead costs that the Company would not incur if not for the capital projects under construction, such as incremental human resources, legal, and power delivery safety. Southern Company Services provides shared services to the Company and includes organizations in project controls, supply chain, engineering, and technology. Costs are recorded in functional cost collector projects.  During the month end close process, these costs are allocated to the appropriate open projects based on capital charges per project, including other indirect capital overheads and adders described in this response. The allocation rate varies by month due to fluctuations in eligible CWIP charges and actual E&S and A&G costs incurred.
The Fleet allocation is applicable to distribution and transmission projects. The allocation is used to allocate these indirect costs associated with maintaining, fueling, depreciating, and managing fleet assets to the business units that utilize fleet vehicles. Vehicles are assigned to allocation groups based on the type of work performed. Costs are recorded in a cost collector project and are allocated to each group based on its proportionate share of the total capitalized cost of all fleet assets. During the month end process, fleet costs allocated to the transmission and distribution groups are further allocated to open projects in alignment with each functional department’s labor charges.
Other indirect capital overheads and adders applied to capital projects include Stores Handling, Minor Materials, Crew Tool, Default Time, and Repair Shop allocations which are applicable to distribution and transmission projects. Please see the Company’s response to STF-SCR-2-12 for further details on the cost collector projects for each of the adders and the basis to which they are applied to allocate to capital projects on a monthly basis.
Allowance for Funds Used During Construction (“AFUDC”) is booked directly to transmission and distribution capital projects based on costs incurred by the Company. The Company calculates the AFUDC Debt and AFUDC Equity rate each month. The rate is calculated according to the FERC CFR Title 18, Part 101, Electric Plant Instructions Section 3(17). These rates are then applied to the base which includes capital costs paid including all indirect capital overheads and adders as of the prior month, half of the current month’s charges, as well as previously incurred AFUDC which is compounded semiannually.
Distribution meters and transformers and Transmission transformers are directly placed in service when purchased and receive the same indirect overhead construction costs and adders as described for other capital projects. Distribution meters and transformers also receive allocated costs to account for the installation labor when they are placed in service. These assets also receive allocated cost of removal upon retirement. A fixed amount is allocated to the associated capital project for each meter or transformer installed or retired each month. Allocation amounts are updated annually based on actual installation and removal costs incurred in the previous year. These allocations record a credit to O&M that is offset when the actual costs are incurred. For Transmission transformers, actual installation and removal costs for specific site locations are added to the capital costs; therefore, no installation or cost of removal allocations need to be applied to Transmission transformers.

question: Is the Company proposing to make any adjustments to the Municipal Franchise Fee, Environmental Cost Recovery Tariff, or Demand Side Management Tariff in response to the other adjustments required in this proceeding? Please explain how any adjustments (or non-adjustments) are in compliance with the ARP Stipulation.
response:
Yes, the Company will propose adjustments to lower the Environmental Cost Recovery (“ECCR”) and Demand Side Management (“DSM”) tariff rider percentages in response to the adjustment of traditional base rate tariffs. The adjustments to these rider tariffs will offset the increase in revenue from those rider tariffs that would have resulted from an increase to traditional base rates for storm recovery as proposed in this filing. No adjustment will be made to the Municipal Franchise Fee (“MFF”) given the percentage of MFF obligation paid to the cities by the Company is directly tied to the total retail revenues collected.
Therefore, the adjustment to base rates for storm cost recovery will have no net impact on ECCR or DSM revenue collections. The adjustments to ECCR and DSM will reduce the collection of revenue from these riders in an amount equal to the increase in revenue that would have resulted from higher traditional base rate tariffs.
While the ARP Stipulation does not specifically contemplate adjustments to these base tariff riders as a result of storm cost recovery, this approach is aligned with the ARP Stipulation language to not adjust base rates except for storm damage costs. Further, the ARP Stipulation provides for the true up of MFF and DSM tariffs until the Company’s next base rate case.

question:
Refer to the response to STF-SCR-1-17 and the statement “capital estimates for storm-related assets are based on actual materials installed and labor estimates required to install those materials.”
Confirm that the capital costs for storm response reflects labor estimates, but does not reflect outside contractor costs. If confirmed, then explain why the capital costs for storm response does not reflect either a mix of labor and outside contractor costs or solely outside contractor costs rather than solely labor estimates.
Refer to the response to STF-SCR-17(d), which states: “actual hours worked to restore a site are tracked and the corresponding labor costs are incorporated into the capital estimate” and notes there is no adder applied to the transmission labor costs.
Indicate whether the “actual labor costs” include both straight time and overtime employee labor costs and are limited to only those costs. If there are other costs, then describe each such cost and how such cost is calculated and included in the capital cost. Provide all supporting documentation.
Indicate whether the Company uses outside line crew contractors, outside vegetation management contractors, outside flagger contractors, and/or outside evaluator contractors. If so, indicate whether any of the contractor cost is capitalized. If so, explain how this cost is determined for capitalization purposes and provide an example. If not, then explain why none of these costs are capitalized.
Refer to STF-SCR-1-17 Attachment.
Provide the underlying terms and a description of each acronym shown on this spreadsheet, including, but not limited to, the CPT, PPP, BBO, and NPT “overheads” that are subtracted from the fully loaded labor costs. In addition, describe why these overheads remain in the regulatory asset after the transfer of the capitalized labor costs.
Explain in detail why none of the staging costs are capitalized to plant.
Explain in detail how the removal costs are calculated.
Explain in detail where the removal costs are charged and confirm the costs are not charged to capitalized storm costs or to the storm reserve (regulatory asset).
response:
Yes, the capital costs related to storms include both internal labor costs and outside contractor costs.
i.  Actual labor costs for transmission storm capital include both straight time and overtime employee labor costs, as well as estimated costs for outside contractors if contractors are used to help restore damaged assets.  Once the direct labor costs are transferred to capital plant account, the capital overhead and other indirect costs are applied similar to other capital costs as described in the Company’s response to STF-SCR-2-11.
ii.   Yes, the Company uses outside line crew contractors, outside vegetation management contractors, outside flagger contractors, and/or outside evaluator contractors to aid with storm restoration. When contractors are brought in to assist with storm recovery, the actual costs associated with any work that are directly tied to capital projects are estimated and capitalized. As part of this process, contractors are grouped according to the function they perform during the storm and are then aggregated and capitalized according to the accounting capitalization policy. For example, the Company capitalizes all of the contractor work to clean up oil spills associated with damaged transformers during storm restoration.
i.  The Distribution capital storm estimate when entered in the system automatically estimates labor adders in the normal course of business to determine the full cost of the capital estimate.  When the Company transfers capital costs from storm O&M and the regulatory asset, those labor adders must be backed out and only the direct labor costs are transferred to ensure the labor adders are not accounted for twice in the capital estimate.  The labor adders removed are:
CPT – Payroll taxes incurred by the Company on employee pay.
PPP – Performance Pay Plan compensation accrued for employees.
BBO – Employee benefits provided to employees.
NPT – Non-productive time (meetings, sick time, etc) incurred in the normal course of business.
These labor adders do not remain in the regulatory asset after the capital transfer.  When the direct labor costs are transferred, the fully loaded labor costs are credited to the regulatory asset, including all associated labor adders.
ii. Staging costs, or logistical costs incurred to support the line crews performing restoration work, are not capitalized.  These costs include such items that would not be capitalized in the normal course of business such as meals, sleeping tents, restroom facilities, security for those sites, etc.
iii. Removal costs are estimated based on the standard removal labor costs (number of hours estimated to complete the work applied to the crew labor rates) and the materials installed during a storm.  A removal cost is recorded for each installation.
iv.  Storm removal costs are charged in the same manner as other capital  removal costs to FERC account 108 per FERC Instructions.  Removal costs related to storm are part of the capitalized storm costs but recorded in FERC account 108 Accumulated Depreciation Reserve rather than FERC account 101 Plant-in-Service.

question:

b. Please explain why this billing did not occur in other storm events identified in MFR 3.
c. Please describe the expenses billed to OATT customers, the nature of OATT customers, and how the amount is calculated.
response:
The amount in the referenced line represents Georgia Power’s portion of Open Access Transmission Tariff (OATT) revenues collected from OATT wholesale transmission customers related to recovery of Hurricane Helene actual transmission storm costs.  For OATT purposes, the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission (FERC) requires actual transmission storm costs to be charged to OATT customers for the year they are incurred. The referenced amount was moved from the regulatory asset balance and expensed to FERC account 573.
All actual transmission storm costs from Southern Company Operating companies (OPCOs) are included in the total OATT revenue requirement to be allocated and charged to OATT customers. Typically, allocation of storm costs for OATT customers are not tracked on an individual basis. Due to the extraordinary nature and magnitude of Hurricane Helene transmission storm costs, the impacts on the OATT rate filing were tracked individually for Hurricane Helene and the Company recorded the transfer from the regulatory asset to non-fuel O&M expense. For all other storms, the transmission storm costs are consolidated with all other costs allocated and charged to OATT customers and are credited to retail cost of service as revenues to offset a portion of the storm accrual expenses approved by the Commission on a monthly basis.
Please see the response to subpart (b) above for storm cost inclusion in the OATT. An OATT customer is an entity that purchases wholesale transmission service from Southern Company under a FERC approved Open Access Transmission Tariff. These customers use the Southern Company transmission infrastructure to move bulk electricity from power generators to their designated destination points. The OATT rates billed to Southern Company OATT customers and the FERC approved Open Access Transmission Tariff are posted on the Southern Company public OASIS site at www.oasis.oati.com/SOCO. Attachment M of the OATT tariff found in the referenced site includes the specific cost inclusion and methodology utilized in determining the OATT rates.  These tariff requirements set by FERC, along with subsequent FERC Orders and Guidance from previous audits of the OATT tariff revenue requirement, are utilized to determine final rates to be collected from OATT customers.
