question:
The following questions refer to restoration times for total loss of service by geographic unit.
What geographic units are used in Georgia Power’s system when determining estimated and actual restoration times (e.g., census blocks, zip-code levels, or a different unit)?
For each geographic unit used by Georgia Power, what was the percent of service restored for the geographic unit compared to the overall system on benchmark time periods used by Georgia Power (e.g., 1-, 2-, 3-days)?
response:
The Company determines Estimated Restoration Times (ERTs) based on outage events identified within the Company’s Outage Management System (OMS). The primary unit used for assigning and managing ERTs is the outage device or outage event as identified within OMS, rather than traditional geographic units such as census blocks, ZIP codes, municipalities, or counties. On normal operating days, ERTs are communicated to affected customers based on device type, location, time of day and other relevant factors, while during larger storm events ERTs are developed at a headquarters or system-wide level and updated as damage assessments are completed and crews arrive on site.
Georgia Power does not benchmark restoration performance by geographic unit, as restoration activities are event‑specific and vary based on storm conditions, damage characteristics, and environmental factors.

question: What percentage of Flat Bill customers currently receive a minimum monthly offer below $50 per month?  Are customers who are at the minimum monthly offer informed that they are receiving an offer above what they would otherwise receive without the minimum requirement?
response:
As of May 2022, 1.8% of current FlatBill participants have a monthly offer that is below $50.  The implementation of the increased minimum offer from $25 to $50 will have no impact on these existing FlatBill customers as long as they remain enrolled in the program. The Company will continue to generate renewal offers for existing participants without applying the new minimum so that they may continue on FlatBill without being impacted by the change.
Regarding offers for new FlatBill customers, the Company is not proposing to make an offer of $50 to customers whose offer falls below the minimum. Rather, the proposed change to the minimum offer will only prevent customers who are not already on FlatBill from receiving an offer, thereby preventing them from enrolling at an amount that is below $50 per month. The Company estimates that this change will exclude approximately 4% of the eligible population from receiving FlatBill offers in the future.

question: Please provide more detailed information regarding the automatic reload option for customers on Prepay and Pay-by-Day programs. Please describe in detail how the automatic reload option works and where this option is available for customers.
response:
Georgia Power customers currently on PrePay or Pay by Day can enroll in Auto Reload, a program that will automatically add money to an account that is estimated to have two days or less of service remaining.
A PrePay or Pay by Day customer will see an icon on their Online Customer Care (OCC) account Overview page with a link to “Manage Auto Reload” where they can manage their saved payment methods by entering credit card and/or debit card information.
Once the payment method information has been saved, the customer can enter the dollar amount of their choice, between $5 and $500, to be automatically charged and applied to their account when it is estimated they have two days or less of service remaining.
Customers may unenroll at any time by removing the dollar amount and/or removing the saved payment method within the Prepay customer portal page.

question: Please describe in detail how the $1.4 million adjustment that was made by the Company regarding the RNR monthly netting pilot was calculated. Please provide all workpapers and calculations to support this adjustment.
response:
The $1.4 million adjustment represents the annual revenue erosion resulting from the overpayment for energy pushed back to the grid once the RNR monthly netting pilot has reached the 5,000-customer limit. Actual participants with 12 months of billing on the pilot through March 2022 formed the basis of the estimate. The data was then scaled up to 5,000 participants based on the list of remaining applicants.

question: Based on the Company's research and analysis or a consultant on its behalf, please provide all examples of jurisdictions or utilities who are eliminating or reducing standard volumetric rate options for residential customers?
response: The Company has not performed a specific analysis of which utilities or jurisdictions are eliminating standard volumetric rate options for residential customers. However, as noted in the Company’s testimony, utilities across the country are moving away from more antiquated volumetric rate designs (such as the R tariff) and toward more modern rate designs that send price signals that more appropriately reflect the cost of service. This trend has been well documented throughout industry press, highlighted at utility conferences, and advanced through regulatory filings for many years. This transition is not isolated to regulated electric utilities but is also prevalent in cooperatives and municipal providers. The Company’s expert witness in the 2019 base rate case, Dr. Ahmad Faruqui, identified utilities that are making this transition and he explained the appropriateness for these new modern rate designs that send more accurate price signals and help achieve the goals of promoting economic efficiency and equity. His testimony goes further to identify different types of modern rate designs and gives specific examples in Table 2 of his testimony of utilities that have experienced success with moving to these improved options. Dr. Faruqui’s testimony remains relevant today and supports the Company’s position of encouraging customers to move to more modern rate structures.

question: Has the Company considered proposing modifications to the standard Residential tariff instead of eliminating the rate option for its new customers? If not, why not? If so, please provide all modifications that have been discussed or analyzed
response:
No, the Company has not considered proposing a structural redesign of the Residential Service rate. Changing the structure of a rate that has 1.7 million customers is not ideal as it is akin to forcing customers onto a new rate, which has the potential to cause material impacts to customer bills and Company revenues.
Closing the Residential Service rate to new residential premises (not to all new customers) allows both customers and the Company an easier and more manageable transition. In a typical year, Georgia Power adds between 25,000 and 30,000 new residential premises, which is just over 1% of the current residential customer population. Customers establishing service at new premises are not influenced by historical bills since they are starting new service at this location. Further, they will have greater access to smart appliances and more efficient building codes to aid in taking advantage of more modern, time-differentiated pricing options.

question: What consideration has the Company given to a time of use residential rate that reflects winter peaks in the system?  Please provide any research or analysis that the Company or a consultant on its behalf has performed.
response:
The Company continually evaluates its pricing options to determine if there should be new rates or modifications to existing rates to send accurate price signals and appropriately collect its costs. At this time, Georgia Power has not identified a need for a winter peak time of use residential rate. This is due to the fact that the Company continues to forecast its peak loads to occur within the summer months. These summer peaks occur during predictable afternoon hours between the months of June through September, which correspond to existing residential time of use offerings.
Unlike when the system peaks during the summer, winter peaks tend to occur infrequently and with a very short duration of one to two hours. The less predictable nature and less frequent occurrence of winter peaks reduces the likelihood of designing an accurate time of use rate design to encourage the correct response from customers that would benefit the system. Therefore, the Company does not support this type of rate design solution at this time.

question: Regarding the one-time interconnection fee for customer generation referenced in Witness Legg’s Testimony on pg. 14, please provide all supporting calculations and workpapers for the selection of $200 as the appropriate amount. Please provide the anticipated revenue this proposed charge would generate for the period of January 1, 2023-December 31, 2025.
response:
As a result of the growth in behind-the-meter (“BTM”) applications for interconnection, the Company has dedicated additional resources and technology solutions to efficiently manage the review, approval, system impact studies and testing of these systems. This $200 fee charged to all BTM projects appropriately collects the known costs directly attributed to processing project applications for interconnection. Georgia Power proposes to no longer charge the $5/kW Witness Testing fee for BTM generators less than 250 kW. The calculated Interconnection Fee averages $190 per application during the next regulatory cycle and includes:
Current project application and interconnection growth trends
Current known costs for PowerClerk (software used to intake BTM applications)
Labor costs associated with general project review and processing; feasibility studies for all size projects; impact and other technical studies for projects less than 250 kW; witness testing for projects less than 250 kW; and special billing set-up and maintenance for all size projects.
The remaining $10 of the $200 fee is an estimate to account for costs not easily quantifiable or attributable on an average per project basis such as: labor associated with program and project inquiries, multiple “truck rolls” for failed witness tests, and additional technology and/or software investments.
During the period of January 1, 2023, through December 31,2025, the estimated revenue collected from this fee is $3.05 million. The revenues and expenses associated with this fee and associated activities will be assigned for recovery through the fuel cost recovery tariff.
Please refer to STF-TAI-1-40 Attachment for additional cost calculation details.

question: Please refer to Rules and Regs, Section F.9. Please explain the reasoning for this new language.  Would this proposed language limit Georgia Power's current liability for damages that arise from voltage surges?  What are Georgia Power's current strategies in limiting voltage surges at customer premises?
response:
The proposed language in the Rules and Regulations Section F.9 helps protect all customers from higher costs by limiting damages in connection with any outage, surge, voltage fluctuation, disturbance or other variation or failure of electric service, or the Company’s equipment, to the extent a cognizable claim arises. This addition complements, but does not restrict, the existing limitation of liability within the Rules and Regulations, which applies to voltage surges as well as other types of damage. The proposed language represents a clarification of current policy and not a change in the current limitation on liability that applies to customer accounts.
To limit voltage surges at customer premises, the Company installs arresters at all overhead transformers, on the overhead lines, and at substations. The Company also installs ground rods at all poles and is increasing the Basic Insulation Level (BIL) of the system as one of the Grid Investments. These strategies work together to limit voltage surges on the system.

question:
Regarding the Charge It-Electric Vehicle rider, referenced in Witness Legg’s Testimony on pg. 16:
Please provide an explanation of how this tariff will “encourage the growth of EVs.”
Why has the Company proposed the mechanism of applying a Billing Demand Adjustment Factor?
If the Billing demand is, according to the CEIV-1 Tariff, “the product of the billing demand as determined by the applicable rate and the Billing Demand Adjustment Factor,” then why does this adjustment factor decrease (and thus the subsidy increase) over time?
Why has the Company chosen 48 months or a 15% Load Factor as an appropriate cutoff for this rider?
Given that this rider will reduce the customer’s bill, what is the Company’s expected loss of revenue as a result of this rider? How will this lost revenue be recovered?
response:
The cost of electricity is one of many considerations that parties interested in providing electric vehicle (“EV”) charging services have to consider when weighing decisions to invest in this new but expanding market. In addition, the availability of public EV charging infrastructure impacts consumers’ willingness to consider the purchase of an EV. The Company is aware of many utilities across the country that have implemented specialized rates to incentivize the investment in new charging infrastructure in their service territories. The new Charge-It Electric Vehicle (CIEV-1) rider provides a program that is on par with what other utilities are offering for energy costs to help ensure Georgia continues to support the EV market and doesn’t fall behind in charging infrastructure development.
The Billing Demand Adjustment Factor allows a transition period for new charging locations to increase the utilization of their capacity.  As this is a nascent market, the state needs early investment in charging infrastructure to support the EVs coming to our roadways, and the CIEV-1 rider will help reduce the concern of initially under-utilized chargers - which can experience high electricity costs under existing rates.
The Company recognizes that the existing wording and structure of the tariff results in the inverse of the intended adjustments to the billing demand. The Company is providing a corrected tariff in STF-TAI-1-51 Attachment. The Billing Demand Adjustment Factor (“BDAF”) is intended to decrease over time, which results in the billing demand returning to the traditional measured billing demand at the end of the 48-month period. However, there is no subsidy with the CIEV-1 rider as it only applies to new loads on the Company’s system and as designed passes the Ratepayer Impact Measure (“RIM”) test. As a result, the new charging loads and the associated revenues will put downward pressure on all customers’ rates.
As indicated in the CIEV-1 tariff, the rider will pair with Power & Light rates, which are among the Company’s most common rates for business applications. Customer loads on the Power & Light rates generally experience a flattening or stabilizing of price (cents per kilowatt hour) once operations reach a 15% load factor. The CIEV-1 tariff was designed to support the expansion of EV chargers, and at a 15% load factor the pricing will stabilize and be more reflective of expected long-term operations. Similarly, the 48-month term of the BDAFs is structured to allow the factors to remain in place for an initial, but also limited, amount of time. Based on expected growth in the EV market, the 48-month period is a reasonable glidepath to allow for the utilization to improve and support the long-term viability of the chargers.
There is no expected loss in revenue from the proposed Charge-It rider. The CIEV-1 rider is only available to new charging loads that expand onto the Company’s system, therefore all sales generated from the rider will be incremental to the Company’s revenues.

question: Please refer to the Company’s Response to STF-TAI-2-2 compared to STF-TAI-1-12.  STF-TAI-2-2 indicates that monthly peak demands are not recorded in the Company’s billing system (except for TOU-RD) such that individual customer maximum demands were not provided. At the same time, response to STF-TAI-1-12 provided hourly demands for every rate schedule. In this regard, please fully explain how the Company calculated (or estimated) each rate schedule’s hourly demand in response to STF-TAI-1-12 when at the same time, the requested demand data was not available for STF-TAI-2-2.  If the hourly demands are not based on actual AMI meter readings, and are estimated, please fully explain how each rate schedule’s hourly demands were estimated in response to STF-TAI-1-12.
response:
The rate schedule hourly demands provided in STF-TAI-1-12 are developed from the Company’s load research studies as discussed in IRP Technical Appendix Section 9.5 and in accordance with industry standard practices. The Company’s standard AMI meter readings, while programed for the accurate determination of billing determinants for rendering bills, are not precise enough to develop individual load profiles that can be summed to represent a rate schedule’s load nor total system load.
The load research studies use sampling methods, including census groups, simple random samples, and stratified random samples to develop representative samples of each rate. Specialized metering equipment capable of more granular energy readings is installed on each selected customer’s premise to collect hourly data for the study period. Load profiles for unmetered rate schedules use assigned profiles. Once the data is collected, hourly demand for each population is estimated using the combined ratio estimation method described in the Association of Edison Illuminating Companies (“AEIC”) Load Research Manual. In the end, each rate is balanced to the total monthly billed energy for that rate and the sum of loads at each hour is balanced to the system load for that hour.
These studies are designed to deliver representative load profiles at the rate level; they cannot determine load profiles for each individual customer. Therefore, the AMI meters and readings are appropriately used for billing individual customers and the Company’s long-standing load research process is appropriately used for developing the hourly demands for rates.

question: Please provide all data, studies and analyses that have been performed by, or on behalf of, the Company regarding cost shifting, revenue erosion, or that indicate rooftop solar customers on the RNR Monthly Netting tariff are not paying their full cost of service.  Please describe in detail how each analysis was performed and provide all studies and analyses in Excel format with formulas intact.
response:
Please see STF-TAI-7 Attachment A and STF-TAI-7 Attachment B for the data, studies, and analyses performed by the Company to evaluate the cost shift from participants in the RNR Monthly Netting pilot.
STF-TAI-7 Attachment A file
Attachment A contains a population of 1,110 RNR Monthly Netting participants who accumulated a full 12 months of experience on the pilot program in 2021. For this sample, the Company gathered the metered readings (both delivered and pushed back energy) from 2021 as well as the installed panel capacities for each customer. The Company was able to estimate the annual usage before solar for each of the 1,110 participants from this data. Using the before solar usages, the customers were then segmented into quartiles.
The Summary tab shows the average estimated annual usage before solar and the average installed panel capacities for the customers within each grouping. These results were used as the basis for selecting residential samples to evaluate the cost shift from the RNR Monthly Netting pilot. The use of residential samples was necessary to perform the detailed analysis since hourly interval usage data is not available for the population of RNR customers, nor does the Company have access to hourly production data for the behind-the-meter solar generators.
STF-TAI-7 Attachment B
Attachment B is a dynamic model that was developed to analyze the cost shift from the RNR Monthly Netting pilot. Based on the quartile groups from STF-TAI-7 Attachment A, the Company selected four representative residential hourly loadshapes, ensuring that each sample closely matched the annual usage profile and did not have solar already installed behind-the-meter. This sampling served as the basis for each quartile’s before-solar hourly loadshape.
Next, an hourly solar load profile was generated from PV Watts based on each sample customer’s specific address and using the panel size for the corresponding average installed solar capacity for each quartile. Each quartile’s before-solar hourly loadshape was netted with the PV watts hourly solar shape to create an after-solar loadshape.
Using the before and after-solar hourly loadshapes, the Company developed the insights and billing determinants applied to the energy-related costs derived from the cost-of-service study to calculate the cost shift associated with the Monthly Netting pilot participants.
The results of the analysis are shown on the Matrix tab where the Company summarizes the cost shift for the Monthly Netting pilot, with results provided for each quartile as well as for the average participant – which was further extrapolated to the 5,000 customer population.

question:
Please refer to the Company’s response to STF-TAI-1, the Company states “The use of residential samples was necessary to perform the detailed analysis since hourly interval usage data is not available for the population of RNR customers, nor does the Company have access to hourly production data for the behind-the-meter solar generators.”
Does the Company have hourly interval usage data for these RNR customers? If so, please explain why the Company did not use the hourly data in its analysis.  If not, please explain why the Company does not have hourly data for these customers.  If it has hourly data for some but not all customers or for some but not all hours, please provide what percentage of customers and hours it has hourly interval data for.
Provide all data, workpapers, and analyses that were used to select the “four representative hourly loadshapes” for Attachment B. Workpapers should be in their original format with formulas intact.
response:
Yes, the Company’s AMI system captures hourly usage data for RNR participants for the general purpose of billing customers based upon their rate plan. Across the residential class, the granularity of this data can vary widely. While most residential customer data is captured at the kilowatt level, the Company also applies meter constants for some while other customers have higher resolution readings that capture usage at sub-kilowatt hour level. Additionally, there are instances when the hourly readings are not received from the meter, thereby creating a gap where usage data is missing for some period of time. As a result of the lack of consistent highly granular data and potential for missing data for actual RNR participants, the Company utilized a more accurate data set with watt-hour level interval data to represent the population of pilot customers.
Please see the Company’s response to STF-TAI-8-9 subpart (a) for the consumption and export data available for RNR customers.

question:
Please refer to the Supplemental Direct Testimony of Lee Evans and Larry Legg on page 13, line 13, which states “Currently, RNR customers do not offset any existing transmission and distribution costs.”
Please provide all analyses and documentation performed by the Company or on its behalf that support this statement.
Do RNR customers offset any future generation capacity costs?  Please explain in detail.
Do RNR customers offset any future transmission costs?  Please explain in detail.
Do RNR customers offset any future distribution costs?  Please explain in detail.
response:
Please refer to STF-TIA-8-13 Attachment, which contains the Final Order in Docket Nos. 4822, 16573, and 19279 resulting from the Commission’s Avoided Costs Review in 2020 and 2021. The proceedings and the related data requests, testimony, and hearings addressed the benefits and costs associated with the RNR rate and collectively are the support for the statements contained in the testimony of Mr. Legg and Mr. Evans.
b.	As stated in the Company’s response to STF-TIA-8-13, generation exported from RNR resources are not included in the Company’s long term capacity planning process. Therefore, there are no avoided generation capacity cost benefits to all customers for these resources. The Company plans to meet future customers’ needs for generation capacity without taking into consideration the generation exported from RNR resources. Currently, a small amount of MW is produced and consumed onsite from RNR customers relative to the planning process. To the extent large amounts of behind-the-meter solar can reliably be planned for to reduce load consumed from the grid, while still complying with necessary IEEE and NERC reliability standards and requirements, it potentially could have an indirect impact in the planning process. However, at this time, the Company cannot speculate on what future value may or may not materialize over decades.
c.	As stated in the Company’s response to STF-TIA-8-13, RNR resources have no long-term, fixed commitment to the Georgia Power System and no obligation to be available to the System. As such, the generation exported from RNR resources is not included in long-term transmission planning and there are no avoided transmission capacity cost benefits to all customers for these resources. The Company plans to meet future customers’ needs for transmission service without taking into consideration the generation exported from RNR resources. NERC reliability standards require that the transmission system be able to serve the load when intermittent behind-the-meter resources are not available. Additional costs could also be required to address the frequency, voltage, system protection, ramping and variability strains these resources put on the system at scale. Currently, a small amount of MW is produced and consumed onsite from RNR customers relative to the planning process. To the extent large amounts of behind-the-meter solar can reliably be planned for to reduce load consumed from the grid, while still complying with necessary IEEE and NERC standards and requirements, it potentially could have an indirect impact in the planning process. However, at this time, the Company cannot speculate on what future value may or may not materialize over decades.
d.  	Based on current IEEE standards, there is no offset to any future distribution costs. Consistent with IEEE-1547, the IEEE Standard for Interconnecting Distributed Resources with Electric Power Systems, Southern Company requires all distributed resources (including solar generation facilities) to cease energizing the distribution system upon occurrence of a fault on the distribution system. These resources are required to stay off-line for up to five minutes after the distribution system voltage and frequency are restored to ranges specified in ANSI standard C84.1. Therefore, the distribution system must be capable of serving 100 percent of the customer’s load during this timeframe. Further, the distribution system must be capable of serving 100 percent of the load when behind-the-meter generation resources are unavailable for any reason. As a result, planning of the distribution system must assume that the feeders containing such generation are still required to carry the full load connected to these circuits, thereby negating any potential deferment of distribution investment, as referenced in the Renewable Cost Benefits Framework filed in the Company’s 2016 and 2019 IRPs in Docket Nos. 40161 and 42310, respectively.

question: Please refer to the Supplemental Direct Testimony of Lee Evans and Larry Legg on page 13, line 16-19, which states “Monthly netting customers rely on the full capacity of the electric system in two critical ways: first, to receive energy from the electric system when their BTM system is not fully offsetting their energy usage, and second, to export energy generated by their BTM system to the grid.” Is it the Company’s position that every RNR customer uses the full capacity of the electric system, including all shared distribution assets, subtransmission assets, and transmission assets, to export energy generated by their BTM system?  If so, please explain in detail how this comports with the physics of the grid where exported energy flows to the nearest load.
response: The energy exported from a behind-the-meter (“BTM”) system will not flow to all parts of the electric system, but a complete electric system is necessary to sustain a demand for the energy pushed back by BTM generation. There is no use for electric service that only provides energy during limited and unpredictable periods when the BTM generation of an adjacent customer exceeds that customer’s load. The assurance of the overall electric system ensures that a proximate customer’s load can make use of exported energy flows because the customer’s load will be met regardless of the availability of pushback of a BTM generator.

question: Please refer to the Supplemental Direct Testimony of Dr. David Gattie on page 6, lines 14-17, which states, “States that have led the way in adopting aggressive net metering strategies as a means to achieve their energy policy goals are now walking back or reevaluating net metering policies, on account of significant negative externalities and issues of ratepayer fairness.”  Please provide a list of states that are “now walking back or reevaluating net metering policies”, including a reference to state laws or utility commission decisions that enacted these policy changes.
response:
The following is a non-exhaustive list of states that have recently reevaluated their net metering policies:
Indiana: In 2017, Indiana signed into law Senate Enrolled Act 309, codified at Indiana Code chapter 8-1-40. This law reversed Indiana’s monthly netting policy, established a path to phasing out net metering altogether by 2047, and allowed utilities to pay solar customers a new rate less than the retail rate known as the “excess distribution generation” (“EDG”) rate. The Indiana Utility Regulatory Commission subsequently approved a proposal in April of 2021, switching from monthly net metering to instantaneous netting in Case No. 45378.
Arizona:  In 2016, the Arizona Corporation Commission (“ACC”) eliminated the state’s retail net metering program. The ACC ordered in Decision No. 75859 that new customer-generators will receive an avoided cost rate for energy exported on an instantaneous basis to the grid. Furthermore, the ACC determined that rooftop solar customers are partial requirements customers who export power to the grid and may be separated into their own rate class for the purposes of assessing additional customer charges for net metering.
Kentucky: In 2019, Kentucky passed Senate Bill 100, which eliminated monthly net metering at the retail electric rate. In May 2021, in Case No. 2020-00174, the Kentucky Public Service Commission implemented a reduced rate for net metering customers specifically by reducing the credit rate for monthly net metering customers from the retail rate to one based on an avoided cost methodology.
New Hampshire: In June 2017, in Order No. 26,029, the New Hampshire Public Utilities Commission reduced the net metering compensation rate from the retail rate to a value equal to 100 percent of the energy and transmission charges and 25 percent of the distribution charge.
Utah: In October 2020, in Docket No. 17-035-61, the Utah Public Service Commission ended net metering and approved a successor tariff that credits distributed generation resources at a reduced export credit rate approved by the Commission.
California: California is in the process of undergoing a multi-year effort to revise the state’s Net Energy Metering (“NEM”) tariff to address high penetration rates and untenable cost shifts to non-participating customers. (Rulemaking (R.) 20-08-020). In December 2021, the California Public Utilities Commission published a proposed decision that features net billing, with instantaneous netting of production and consumption as opposed to hourly netting and requires customers to switch to specific, high-differential TOU billing plans and implements reduced compensation for excess energy. The proposed decision has not been finalized and is still under consideration.

The Company’s experience has indicated the need to limit interconnection capacity or require system upgrades or customer mitigation, as needed.
Complications that the Company is concerned with regarding DER interconnection are included in Section A5.0 in STF-WG-1-1 Attachment F.
Additional complications that the Company has experienced with DER interconnection relate to:
Need for System Upgrades – System upgrades such as reconductoring, upgrading of protective devices, adding voltage regulators, and adding Direct Transfer Trip are sometimes required for a distribution feeder to accommodate a DER of certain size without voltage violations, thermal and interrupting limit violations, devices failure, customer equipment failure, and other safety related issues
Coordination of protective devices – Traditional distribution protective devices and their coordination are designed for one-way radial power flow. The addition of DERs into a circuit introduces sources that make two-way power flow possible. Moreover, some DERs require interconnection transformer configuration that also introduces ground sources into the circuit that may adversely affect substation protective devices, which sometimes renders them useless. Therefore, anytime a DER is added into a circuit, a complete short circuit study and protection coordination study of the protective devices is performed to identify issues. These problems can be mitigated by changing settings, adding devices, and introducing transfer trip schemes.
Voltage Excursions – Anytime a DER is added into a circuit, the terminal voltage at the point of common coupling increases. This increase in voltage sometimes ends up violating the voltage limit that adversely affects customers on the same circuit, which could lead to equipment failure. If all other ways to address the problem are exhausted, limiting active power output of the DER is used to keep the voltage below the American National Standards Institute (ANSI) upper voltage limit.
Radio Frequency Interference – This is a phenomenon that the Company experienced on central inverter-based DERs that require an ungrounded transformer on the DER side. Such installations introduce Radio Frequency Interference into the distribution ground wire, which affects users of lower range of AM band frequency. This frequency range is usually used by airport communication systems and AM band radio listeners. These issues are addressed using filters to block the specific frequency signals.
Harmonic Distortion – Inverter-based DERs are prone to generating harmonics due to high frequency power electronics switching involved in producing a matching voltage and frequency signal to the grid. Harmonics are also dependent on the settings and firmware that DERs use. In cases where high harmonics injections are detected during witness testing, settings and firmware changes have been used to address these problems.
Power Factor Limitation – On some circuits where the addition of DERs introduce upper limit voltage violations, power factor limitation is applied to avoid major circuit upgrades. By introducing an “absorbing” power factor, the DERs absorb reactive power and keep the voltage below the upper limit while producing and exporting active power to the grid.
The Company will continue to utilize its internal power quality and reliability subject matter experts, who are actively engaged in national code and standards development, to ensure that DER interconnection continues to meet required voltage and thermal standards.

As noted in the referenced “Customer Benefit Study of Distribution Investment,” based on the Company’s analysis in 2019, the Company expected the system-wide SAIDI to reach approximately 65 in 2031 if the distribution investment plan was implemented over the 2020-2030 period. For residential load, growth can occur through increased use in home additions/remodeling, vehicle charging, new home construction and changing work habits/locations (as seen with increased work from home trends). Also, for residential customers, load reduction can occur through implementation of more efficient appliances and home systems (HVAC, etc.). The number of poles worked on can be considered a proxy for pole arms replaced (both wood and steel) and/or wildlife protectors installed and is included in the referenced attachment.

As such, counts of pole arms, trip savers, and/or wildlife protectors for projects where final scoping and engineering are not yet complete are estimates based on similar historical projects.
(i) Fiberglass pole arms provide improved electrical insulation over wood, thereby improving reliability by reducing flashover events. Unlike wood, fiberglass pole arms do not rot, are not susceptible to damage caused by insects, and are more fire resistant. Further, fiberglass arms offer resilience advantages in that they tend to break away from a pole when a heavy load such as a tree falls on a distribution line. The fiberglass arm’s tendency to fail before the pole fails results in fewer broken poles during storms that topple trees and other heavy debris into distribution lines.

Refer to the Company’s reliability performance generally.  Please provide:

response:
The Company’s inspection program and replacement policies for poles and structures are outlined in STF-WG-1-27 Attachments A through E.
The Company’s vegetation management plan for transmission and distribution is as follows:
Transmission Herbicide – Work plan consists of one-third system miles to be sprayed each year.
Reclearing – Work plan is based on approximately one-sixth of system miles.
Yard Tree Removal - Scheduled based on the forester’s assessment of the condition of lines within their territories, with respect to planted incompatible species in the right of way (“ROW”). Lines that are most heavily impacted, and where conductor clearance is approaching critical, are prioritized highest. In highly urbanized areas, yard tree removal should be performed approximately every ten years.
Danger Tree – At least one patrol on all transmission lines.
Transmission Side Tree Trimming - Established work plan determined by due date of next scheduled activity for each line and the criticality of the line; critical lines are high voltage bulk lines. Cycle is 8-12 years based on vegetation type and right of way conditions.
Transmission Urban Tree Trimming - Established work plan determined by due date of next scheduled activity for each line. Cycle is an average of three years based on vegetation type and right of way conditions.
Distribution Herbicide – Work plan is based on a two-year cycle where approximately half of the system miles are sprayed each year.
Distribution Tree Trimming – Cycle typically ranges from 24-60 months, with an average of approximately three and a half years. Schedules are based on vegetation type and ROW conditions.
Distribution feeder performance is quantified using 24 months of outage data. The feeders are ranked according to their annualized number of customers interrupted (“CI”) and annualized customer minutes of interruption (CMI) over the 24-month period. The worst ranked feeder by CI is assigned a CI rank of (1), the second worst is assigned a CI rank of (2), and so on. Similarly, the worst ranked feeder by CMI is assigned a CMI rank of (1), the second worst is assigned a CMI rank of (2), and so on. Each feeder is then given a reliability score that is the sum of its CI rank and CMI rank. The worst performing feeders are those with the lowest reliability score. Feeders are removed from consideration if they were the subject of a reliability project in the previous two years. Feeders identified by the Grid Investment Plan can also be removed from consideration. The remaining worst performing feeders are candidates for the next annual work plan.

question:
Refer to the Company’s reliability generally. Provide typical protection settings (i.e. Number of counts to lockout; type of trip settings such as 1 fast trip, 3 slow trips etc; and duration of outage time between trips) for each of the following devices:
Feeder Breakers
Reclosers
Sectionalizers
TripSavers/FuseSavers
Any other automated distribution switching devices.
response:
Feeder Breakers
Overhead Feeder: The typical operation of a breaker is 4 total trips with open intervals of 2 seconds, 15 seconds, then 30 seconds between trips. The first trip is generally a faster response to the fault than the subsequent delay trips.
Underground Feeder: A predominantly underground feeder can be set with reclose attempts prior to lockout depending on the unique attributes of the feeder. For 2 trip breakers, the open interval is 10 seconds. For 3 trip breakers, it is 2 seconds and 15 seconds.
Reclosers
Overhead Feeder:
Communicating Electronic Recloser: The typical operation of communicating electronic reclosers is 4 total trips with the first two being faster responses than the next two (2 fast-2 delay). Open intervals between trips would be 2 seconds, 10 seconds, and 10 seconds.
Hydraulic Recloser: These devices have the same operation as electronic reclosers (2 fast-2 delay) except the open intervals are 2 seconds, 2 seconds, and 2 seconds.
Underground Feeder:
Electronic Recloser: Typical operation is 2 total trips with a delayed response to allow for other downstream devices to operate. The open interval between trips is typically 10 seconds.
Sectionalizers
Overhead Feeder: These devices are programmed to count for fault current and loss of voltage from the upstream tripping device. A 2-count or 3-count would be typical before the device trips.
Underground Feeder: These devices will trip with one count of fault current and loss of voltage.
TripSavers: These devices are the same operationally as electronic reclosers (2 fast - 2 delay) except the open intervals are 2 seconds, 5 seconds, and 5 seconds.
Any other automated distribution switching devices.
Underground Feeder: Vacuum fault interrupter: These are part of larger pad-mounted switchgear and interrupt faults by tripping only once. They do not reclose.
Other non-communicating electronic reclosers: These devices typically have the same operation as TripSavers.

question: Refer to the Company’s distribution planning and operations processes generally.  Provide a list of software systems (Cyme, Synergy, SCADA, ADMS, etc.) used to model system load flow and performance, and to operate the system from distribution control centers. Please identify the software developer/version, explain how the Company uses each such software system, the capabilities available from each, and the types of analyses typically performed using each.
response:
The Company uses CYME International's CYMDIST 8.2 r5 software to model its distribution system. This tool is used to perform unbalanced load flow analysis to detect low voltage, phase balancing, power factor correction-optimal capacitor placement along with sizing, short circuit analysis, motor starting, and evaluation for distributed generation (“DG”) interconnection impacts. CYMDIST uses load allocation integration derived from GIS circuit models in conjunction with specific customer load data as needed to create the modeling platform.
The Company uses one vendor solution for its outage management and distribution management systems (“OMS” and “DMS,” respectively) and a second vendor solution for its SCADA system, as detailed further below. An integration between the two systems provides Advanced Distribution Management System (“ADMS”) functionality in distribution control centers.
The OMS and DMS solutions are provided in a single product, Oracle’s Network Management System (“NMS”). The Company currently operates on NMS version 2.3. NMS uses power off messages from AMI meters and outage reports from customers to predict which devices along a distribution feeder are faulted. Outage events are also generated from SCADA telemetry. The outage predictions are presented to control center operators for dispatch to field employees who respond to outages. Control center operators have two digital models of the electric distribution system at their disposal within NMS:
The NMS Operational Model is a digital model of the distribution grid. It receives real time or near real time data from SCADA, AMI, the customer information system, vehicle locating, and crew status to present information to the operator. It is the real time power flow model and outage device prediction engine. It also contains load models for customers and has the ability to include DERs in the power flow model.
NMS Study Mode is a digital twin of the NMS Operational Model. It mimics the current state of the operational model (and thus the current state of the system) and can also mimic the nominal state. Operators use Study Mode to model various scenarios prior to selecting and executing operational plans on the actual distribution grid.
Operators validate, secure, and issue safety documents within NMS. Switching operations are planned, executed, and modeled within NMS. During the modeling of possible switching operations, NMS predicts power flow resulting from the operation and identifies constraints that would be at risk of violation. When a telemetered distribution device trips due to a fault, NMS consumes the fault data from the device and predicts possible fault locations for the operator, which enables reduced patrol times during outages. Outage information that is communicated to customers is first captured in NMS before being pushed to Georgia Power’s outage communication channels through various interfaces.
The distribution SCADA infrastructure is made up of a suite of applications provided by General Electric (“GE”), including Habitat 5.10 SP1, SCADA 3.1 SP1, APF 3.1 SP1, Browser 4.1 SP1, and Comm 3.1. These tools work in tandem to provide near-real-time information to system operators and the ability to issue control to field devices. The GE Comm product is used to send near-real-time data to the Oracle NMS infrastructure and exchange near-real-time data with the Transmission SCADA infrastructure. In addition to the GE applications, the Company uses Minsait ACS’s Prism 11.30 application to provide automated fault location, isolation, and service restoration capability.

The benefits of DERMS described in STF-WG-1-1 Attachment D are not being fully extracted from the Company’s current grid management applications. Without DERMS, current tools in use will be insufficient to manage the substantial number of DER expected to connect to the grid.  Restricted only to current tools, a system operator may be able to utilize a specific DER site to deliver hyper-local benefits to the grid in solving a particular grid constraint that may only be present for a relatively short period. In contrast, a fully integrated DERMS unlocks the potential to continually optimize larger portions of the grid and solve for a variety of constraints, such as economic dispatch and voltage control. These optimization engines are expected to effectively consume the number of data streams available from a grid with hundreds or thousands of discrete DER interconnections and thereby allow system operators to deliver more benefits offered by DER. These data streams would be overwhelming to a single system operator trying to manage the grid in the absence of DERMS.
The Company’s Interconnection (“IC”) Process described in Section 8.0 of STF-WG-1-1 Attachment F is used to manage potential complications of DER. Major components of the IC Process related to management of DER potential complications include: (i) DER Impact Study; (ii) Interconnection Equipment Study; (iii) Interconnection Agreement Execution; (iv) Interconnection Equipment Installation; (v) DER Interconnection Protection Settings Review; and (vi) DER Witness Testing.
DER Witness Testing is used to manage potential complications related to (i) Current/Harmonic Distortion and (ii) Radio Frequency Interference.
All other potential complications, including (iii) Unintentional Islanding, (iv) Equipment Ratings, (v) Voltage Regulation, (vi) System Protection (including coordination of protective devices), (vii) Instantaneous Overvoltage and (viii) Rapid Voltage Changes, and (x) Flicker, are handled through all phases of the IC Process mentioned above beginning with performance of DER Impact Studies. These studies identify potential complication(s) and their solutions, which could involve the addition of new electric/communication system equipment or upgrades to existing electric system equipment. Following identification of solutions to potential complications, an Interconnection Equipment Study is performed to determine estimated cost of implementing all solutions. The cost is presented to the DER Owner. Following acceptance of Interconnection Proposal by and Notice to Proceed from the DER Owner, the remaining phases of the IC Process are then executed to grant DER Parallel Operation permission.
The volume of DER adoption will drive an increase in the rates of changes to the state of the grid. As more DERs are added to the system, it becomes increasingly important to have awareness of these assets as they affect the load the system must serve. This awareness can help the Company better optimize around these DER assets with the fleet generation assets. A system operator will not be able to process all the information coming in and make decisions fast enough to optimize the grid. Furthermore, those decisions cannot be made by a human on a grid-level scale. DERMS will be necessary to begin introducing the task of balancing generation capacity and load on the grid to distribution system operators. The Company’s implementation of DERMS will allow for maturation of the solution before hundreds or thousands of additional discrete DER are connected to the grid. The Company envisions all customer generation sized 250 kilowatts and above to be installed with communications capabilities that allow visibility and control by the Company. It is conceivable that this threshold could be lowered in the future, thereby opening the door for an even greater number of DER that need to be optimized on the distribution grid.  Furthermore, DERMS is an enabling technology to consider demand-side resources alongside supply-side resources in future IRPs, as ordered by the Commission in the 2022 IRP in Docket No. 44160. DERMS functionality is necessary to effectively dispatch these demand-side resources in a manner that delivers their full benefits to customers.
The Company completed a limited DERMS deployment in 2018-2019 with Advanced Control Systems (“ACS”). The ACS solution was applied to a feeder that hosts a solar site at the University of Georgia. The pilot demonstrated that the system could connect to a controller at the solar site and the distribution capacitors along the feeder. The system could interact with the solar site control and the capacitors to manage voltage along the feeder.
The Company’s Tech Square microgrid that was approved by the Commission began operation in 2021. The microgrid is an urban microgrid demonstration and is connected to an underground network, a traditional distribution feeder, and loads in the adjacent building. The microgrid incorporates a fuel cell, battery storage, and diesel and natural gas generators.
The Company’s DER offerings have given rise to numerous DER sites that are interconnected to various points of the Company’s distribution grid. Those DER sites operate in parallel with the distribution system, as described in STF-WG-1-1 Attachment F.

In 2021, the Electric Power Research Institute performed a comparative assessment of leading DERMS product vendors and developed this document to better understand what DERMS functionalities vendors had at the time along with future plans for each product offering. The Company has met with several of the vendors mentioned in this document.
The Company is pursuing a DERMS solution to develop an enterprise-wide approach to implementing and operating variable energy resources and DER. This framework is cognizant of and informed by the efforts described in the response to subpart ‘d’ above. The Company has released a DERMS Request for Information (“RFI”). The responses received from the RFI will further inform the Company’s requirements for an integrated DERMS.
A DERMS solution is a natural and logical step for a utility facing large growth in renewable and other DER resources. The Company views the alternative to DERMS being a posture where DER interconnections are restricted because of human limitations in managing and responding to additional data streams coming from the distribution grid. If DER growth is unrestricted without the benefit of DERMS, the utility risks a loss of grid control, which would compromise grid reliability and stability. A DERMS solution implemented alongside a growth in DER interconnections positions the Company to deliver the full intended benefits of DER at the time of interconnection without compromising grid reliability and stability.

question:
Refer to the Company’s response to STF-WG-1-8 (f), which states “The Company evaluates improvements at the system level to provide the greatest benefit to all customers instead of at the solution level. Therefore, no cost-benefit analyses were performed at the Package level.”
If no cost-benefit analyses were performed at the Package level, explain how the Company knows whether or not any particular Package delivers benefits to customers in excess of costs to customers.
If no cost-benefit analyses were performed at the Package level, and the Company has no understanding of the relative benefits of one Package vs. another, explain how the Company can determine the optimum mix of spending among the available Packages.
Page 6 of the Attachment to the Company’s TS response to STF-REC-1-1 refers to an “REDACTED”. Provide this model in MS Excel spreadsheet format with no hidden or protected cells and all formulae working and available for Staff review.
Refer to the Company’s response to subpart (c) above. If the model is not available in MS Excel format, provide all model details and descriptions sufficient to allow Staff to operate the model. Also, provide model inputs and outputs for five circuits selected at random.
response:
As stated in the Company’s response to STF-REC-1-1 and during the discovery conference GPC held with Staff on Monday, August 15, the Company performs an Economic Benefit Analysis, not a Cost Benefit Analysis. In the Economic Benefit Analysis, the Company minimizes the total cost to the customer for outages including economic costs from outages, O&M costs to maintain and repair the system and direct costs of new investments. The Economic Benefit Analysis evaluates the total cost to customers across numerous different investment scenarios to determine the plan that minimizes the total cost to customers across the system.
Further, the Economic Benefit Analysis determines the total cost to customers across the system based on a set of circuit and package combinations versus a package level. It would be irrelevant to complete a Cost Benefit Analysis at a package level as the drivers of cost and reliability improvement vary by circuit. As the physical characteristics of each circuit vary, the associated costs, in absolute terms, from a package applied to an individual circuit will also vary. Similarly, the starting SAIDI / SAIFI of each circuit also varies, and, as a result, so does the reliability improvement realized from applying a package to a circuit. As a result, it is not possible to calculate a package level benefit.
As demonstrated in Table I.4 in the Company’s response to STF-REC-1-1, the Company has a quantified understanding of the relative reliability benefits of applying each investment package to relevant circuits (i.e., those that meet the qualification criteria laid out in Table I.2 of STF-REC-1-1). The Company evaluates different combinations of potential investment packages to determine which subset of investments produces the lowest total cost to the customer, at the system level, for a given SAIDI. The Company then compares the total cost to the customer, at the system level, across SAIDIs to determine the optimal investment scenario as described in additional detail in STF-REC-1-1.

response:

Please refer to the Company’s response to STF-WG-1-13 (b), which states, “[t]hese end state reliability estimates were developed by analyzing existing feeders that were already 90% or more undergrounded; therefore, the completion date is not applicable.” The Company had not previously deployed undergrounding conversions at the scale evaluated in the Grid Investment Program. As mentioned, the Company, looked to circuits that were already underground to understand their reliability performance. These underground circuits were not reliability projects; some were initially constructed as underground feeders and others had sections of underground cable appended to them to connect new customers. In the Company’s response to STF-WG-1-8 Attachment, the 30 circuits listed under the package “Basic Insulation Level” on Excel rows 27 through 56 are the same projects as “Circuit Hardening,”. The packages deployed by the Company were designed to improve non-MED or “blue sky” reliability performance. As referenced in Section I.A. of STF-REC-1-1, the Company worked with relevant engineering experts who had experience across the Company’s system to identify the circuit designs that improved reliability driven by specific outage drivers. This was done without considering major event days.
The SAIDI and SAIFI improvement estimates are for non-MED or “blue sky” reliability. As explained in the Company’s response to STF-WG-1-8 (a), the improvements were calculated based on similar, but smaller scale investments made in the past. As these estimates already remove MED days, MED improvements are not factored into the improvement estimates.
As referenced above, and in Section I.D. of STF-REC-1-1, major weather events were not considered in the development of the reliability improvements.
It is important to note that packages can be applied to circuits whose five-year average reliability is in the third or fourth quartile. Therefore, the five-year average SAIDI and SAIFI are less than the median, not the average across all circuits. Lastly, it is important to note that the median and fourth quartile thresholds have held constant since the 2019 base rate case and have not been updated for current reliability, which is worse overall than in the 2019 base rate case.
As shown in Table 1.4, the Company estimates improvements by applying a percentage reduction from the starting SAIDI and SAIFI of the circuit. Therefore, a circuit with a higher starting SAIDI or SAIFI will have a larger numerical reduction in SAIDI or SAIFI than circuits with lower starting SAIDI or SAIFI given the same percentage improvement. By using a percentage improvement for these overhead packages rather than numerical values, the Company compensates for the differences in starting performance of each feeder.

question:
Refer to the Company’s TS response to STF-REC-1-1 (A Customer Benefit Study of Distribution Investment). Page 3 states “REDACTED.” Refer also to the Company’s response to STF-WG-1-27 (b), which describes the Company’s vegetation management efforts.
The Company’s distribution investment plan consists of applying capital-intensive “packages” to addressing circuits with third and fourth quartile reliability performance. Provide any analyses the Company has completed to compare the benefits and costs of more aggressive vegetation management practices to the benefits and costs of various packages. If the Company has not completed such analyses or comparisons, please explain why not.
Please provide any vegetation management program benchmarking efforts (costs, planning practices, operating practices, cycle frequency, performance, etc.) the Company has conducted since 2015.
Provide a list of circuits for which routine tree trimming and line clearing/reclearing activities were completed by year from 2012 to 2021.  For each circuit listed, provide the line miles cleared in each year.
Please provide at least five examples of “REDACTED” the Company aims to cure through its application of capital-intensive packages. For each REDACTED, describe the deficiencies and quantify the associated financial and/or reliability consequences for customers.
response:
The Company developed the Grid Investment Plan to deploy more permanent and effective solutions to improve reliability and lower the total economic cost to the customer. Routine vegetation management solutions are only effective temporarily. Additionally, many of the vegetation management-related outages that are experienced on the Distribution system are from off the right-of-way where the Company has no rights to trim. Given these reasons and the additional operation and maintenance costs to customers, incremental vegetation management solutions were not considered as part of the Grid Investment Plan package options.
The Company has not engaged in any third-party vegetation management program benchmarking efforts since 2015.
Please refer to STF-WG-2-16 Attachment.
Five examples of legacy design specifications addressed through the Grid Investment Plan include:
Replacing wood and steel pole hardware with fiberglass, and porcelain insulators with polymer insulators.
Deficiency: Insufficient basic insulation level relative to better insulators and pole hardware, resulting in more frequent outages.
Quantification of impact: Components with higher BIL are expected to improve the line performance SAIDI by 20% and SAIFI by 30% over grounded steel arms. This will increase the reliability and resilience of the line by reducing lighting over-voltage outages.
Increasing spacing between conductors.
Deficiency: Close spacing between conductors increases the risk of phases coming in contact with each other or other equipment and increases the risk of debris getting between phases.
Quantification of impact: Increased spacing by adding larger arms. Wider brackets will reduce phase-to-phase contact by wildlife, trees, or conductor contact due to wind, vehicular damage, or other times when closer spacing allows adjacent conductors to come into contact. This will improve the reliability by reducing breaker and recloser operations as well as reducing permanent outages caused by line contact.
In strategic locations, replacing fuses with Trip Savers.
Deficiency: Fuses, relative to Trip Savers, do not restore temporary faults.
Quantification of impact: Trip Savers allow a temporary fault to clear in many instances and restore service as 50-90% of faults, like lightning, wildlife contact, and trees brushing the line during wind events, are cleared during the reclosing cycle while all fuse operations including those for temporary faults, result in a permanent outage.
Replacing manual devices with automated devices and adding additional automation devices strategically.
Deficiency: Manual devices, relative to automated devices, do not allow for automatic fault isolation and restoration and take longer to restore power to customers.
Quantification of impact: Automated devices will operate and our fault location, isolation, and service restoration (“FLISR”) schemes will segment the outage and re-route and restore service in less than a minute in cases where these schemes are used.
Decreasing number of customers per section.
Deficiency: Having more customers between protective devices increases the number of customers who experience an outage when faults occur.
Quantification of impact: Adding devices for segmentation reduces the number of customers experiencing a permanent outage and reduces SAIDI by eliminating large numbers of customers impacted in each section.

question: Refer to TS Attachment provided in response to STF-REC-1-1. Staff notes that REDACTED was not an option or Package made available to the Regions as part of the Company’s reliability improvement efforts. Please explain why this common approach to reliability improvement was not included as an option or Package made available.
response:
The Company maintains and executes a routine vegetation management program to account for routine clearing of the right of way (and removal of dead or harmful trees that could cause outages). The Grid Investment Plan was developed to prevent outages that occur despite this program (e.g., healthy trees falling from outside of the right of way that cause blue sky outages) and therefore, additional routine vegetation management was not considered.
Where possible and advantageous, the Company considers and will purchase additional right of ways for both the Grid Investment Plan and traditional Transmission and Distribution to provide extra clearance between vegetation and the line. However, this solution cannot be applied systematically as it relies on multiple right of way acquisitions from all landowners and creates ongoing O&M expenses to maintain the acquired right of ways. Therefore, the Company decided not to include expanded vegetation management as a package.

The cutoff point for the number of worst performing feeder projects is driven by the funding available for the overall program each year. Feeders are selected for review based on their reliability score, as described in the Company’s response to STF-WG-1-27 part ‘c’. There is not a target percentage or number of feeders, nor is there a threshold of CI or CMI performance above which all feeders are selected for review. The reliability score method identifies those feeders that make the largest contribution to Company level SAIDI and SAIFI performance. The reliability score is calculated at the substation breaker level. During the development of a worst performing feeder project, the Company will typically examine outage patterns and the greatest sources of poor performance. The proposed project is designed to address those findings.

question:
Refer to the Company’s responses to STF-WG-1-27 (d), which describe the Company’s substation equipment testing programs.
Please describe the purpose/goal/objective of the Company’s substation equipment testing programs.
Please describe the process, including steps and timelines, the Company follows when a piece of substation equipment fails its tests.
Please confirm that the capital budgets for replacing substation equipment that fails equipment tests are found in “Capital Maintenance” budgets. If this cannot be explained, please identify where the Company budgets for replacing substation equipment that has failed its tests lies.
response:
The purpose of maintaining and testing substation equipment is to ensure that substation equipment will perform reliably while it is providing service to customers and to ensure the safety of the general public and Company employees. These practices are also intended to extend the life of system assets for as long as practical without jeopardizing system reliability.
When an item of substation equipment fails a test, the Company will repeat the test after the verification of the general test parameters for the equipment that is being tested. If the repair needed for the equipment is not evident or practical, the personnel conducting the test will contact the appropriate Subject Matter Expert (“SME”) for the equipment being tested. The SME will review the equipment being tested, the test(s) performed, test methods, test results, and then determine if additional diagnostic tests should be performed. After test results and methods are reviewed and analyzed by the SME, a decision will be made to repair or replace the equipment.
With the exception of substation class transformers, which are captured in the “Commitments” investment category, the replacement costs of substation equipment that fails equipment tests are captured in the “Capital Maintenance” budgets.

question:
Refer to the Company’s response to STF-WG-1-28 (e), which states “The Company does not maintain projected net-book values at a substation level or forecast for the retirement of specific assets.”
This statement appears to indicate that, for substation equipment removed from service as part of a substation rebuild, partial rebuild, or equipment replacement package, the Company made no changes to the revenue requirement in this rate case associated with any net book value remaining on such equipment. For example, one could argue that a customer should not continue to pay a rate of return, or income taxes on that return, for the net book value of an asset that is no longer in service, or depreciation on an asset that is no longer in service. Please indicate where in this rate case’s revenue requirement calculations the Company has made any reductions in the revenue requirement for equipment with net book value removed from service due to the application of a substation package. If the Company has made no such revenue requirement adjustment, please explain why not.
This statement indicates the Company is not complying with generally accepted accounting principles. Group accounting is typically reserved for asset types that are large in number but of small value individually, such as meters. Substation equipment, from switches to circuit breakers to power transformers, are typically purchased for tens of thousands, hundreds of thousands, or millions of dollars each. Individual asset accounting is typically employed for large-dollar equipment, which means that the Company should be able to answer STF-WG-1-28(e). Please answer this data request as submitted, or explain why the Company does not maintain individual asset records for large dollar substation equipment.
response:
Retirements for substations are budgeted at the functional level and not by individual substations. The Company’s projected plant-in-service balances for transmission and distribution shown in Exhibit___ (APA/SPA/ADH/MBR-1, Schedule 1 Total Company) include projected closures net of retirements.
When an asset is retired, FERC accounting dictates removal of the gross plant investment from plant in service (FERC account 101) and any unrecovered costs, or remaining net book value, are recorded to accumulated depreciation (FERC account 108). Therefore, retirements do not impact net plant in service in rate base and the associated return. The accumulated depreciation reserve balance, including any over or under-recovered net book value from retired assets, is considered in the development of the depreciation rates within the depreciation study to appropriately recover the full capital investments incurred in the provision of electric service. The Company follows group depreciation and accumulated depreciation is recovered over the group’s average service life.
The Company complies with Generally Accepted Accounting Principles (“GAAP”) and maintains specific asset records as it pertains to its substations’ equipment and cost of its investment on an actual basis. STF-WG-1-28 (e) requests “[f]or each substation listed as part of type ‘rebuild’ [expected to be completed by December 31, 2022], provide a list of equipment removed from service and the net book value of each at the time removed from service.”
No rebuilds in the list of substations have been completed as of August 2022. Therefore, no specific net book values have been calculated at this time.
