question:
Please refer to the Company's response to DR STF-REC-1-7-c: It states: "The Company uses condition-based maintenance ("CBM") tools to monitor and assess data for various transmission substation equipment. Equipment that is currently monitored on the system includes transformers, breakers, and substation batteries.”
Please describe in detail, with examples, the CBM tools used to predict and assess data for various substation equipment.
Please describe in detail the processes and tools used to monitor and assess the physical condition of transmission lines, such as towers/poles, conductors, and other components related to transmission lines.
Please explain whether CBM tools and the results they provide can determine the expected life of substation equipment, either by equipment type or by pieces of equipment individually.
Please explain whether CBM tools can be used to extend the useful life of substation equipment beyond industry standards? Give examples where this was done. If not, please explain.
response:
Transformer Monitoring
Dissolved Gas Analysis (“DGA”) Monitor
DGA is a test performed to access the transformer health. The fundamental purpose of DGA is to distinguish between normal and abnormal conditions. Transformers with on-line DGA monitors monitor the dissolved gasses in the transformer and alarm when gases are detected outside of normal and expected limits based on standards such as IEEE C57.104, Roger Ratio, and Duval’s Triangle. When a DGA on-line monitor indicates an alarm, a follow-up on-site/physical sample lab test is performed to verify on-line DGA monitor results. When a DGA lab sample has DGA results with any key gases (such as Acetylene (C2H2), Ethylene (C2H4), Carbon Monoxide (CO), and Hydrogen (H2)) above acceptable limits, the transformer is removed from service for inspection, evaluation, and off-line testing (such as power factor, transformer turns ratio (“TTR”), winding resistance, and Megger Core testing).
Bushing Monitor
The Company uses on-line bushing monitors to monitor the bushings on power transformers. It is important to note that bushing failures are a leading cause of transformer failures. The bushing monitors monitor the power factor and C1 capacitance of condenser style bushings, based on the manufacturer and nameplate data on the bushing. Limits on power factor and C1 capacitance (the main insulation of the bushing) are typically determined by the manufacturer. Any change in ether power factor or capacitance will indicate an alarm. Based on the level of the reading and/or the rate of change of power factor and/or capacitance, the measured values will be sent to a Company transformer bushing SME to analyze. Once the SME analyzes this data, a decision is made to either continue monitoring the bushing or de-energize the transformer for further evaluation and testing.
Infrared Monitor
The Company uses infrared cameras (“IR”) to monitor arresters, bushings, and oil compartment/radiator temperatures. Temperature is an early indicator of bushing and arrester issues and another measure, to be used in conjunction with on-line bushing and on-line DGA monitoring on power transformers, to determine the overall health of the transformer. The IR cameras are set up to monitor the arrester and bushing reference temperature and polygons are drawn and setup within the camera software on the arrester and bushings to monitor and determine if the temperature exceeds normal expected operating temperatures. If a temperature on an arrester, bushing and/or oil compartment/radiators indicate a high temperature, a Company transformer subject matter expert (“SME”) will be consulted. The SME will either indicate further monitoring or have the transformer removed from service for further off-line testing and evaluation. Once off-line evaluation and testing is complete, a decision is made to either return the transformer to service or replace the transformer.
Breaker Monitoring
The current circuit breaker monitoring is performed on the parameters of the Schweitzer Engineering Laboratories (SEL) 351 Overcurrent/Ground Relay. The Company developed internal software to compare the published nameplate Mechanical Trip/Open Time Limit to the Mechanical Trip Time measured during the trip operation event. If the difference is outside the trip/open limits, the software produces a report for the Company’s substation support team. A Company breaker SME then evaluates mechanical trip times. Based on the breaker type, breaker location, breaker mechanism type, and the mechanical trip time, the SME will either recommend further monitoring or have the breaker removed from service for further off-line testing and evaluation. Once offline testing and evaluation of the breaker is complete, a decision is made to either repair or replace the breaker.
Battery Monitoring
Battery monitoring systems enable maintenance personnel to better determine the health and operating condition of substation battery systems, which are critical to the safe and reliable operation of the electric system. The Company is in the process installing battery monitors on NERC/CIP substation battery systems. Recent changes to the North American Electric Reliability Corporation’s (“NERC”) Protection System Maintenance requirements (PRC-005-2) have placed new importance on these critical systems by including strict inspection, testing, and maintenance requirements for bulk electric system battery systems. Per NERC requirements, the Company monitors the following parameters:
String Voltage: Provides high and low monitoring and alarming of string voltage at the battery positive and negative terminals.
Ground Fault: Provides monitoring and alarming for unintentional DC ground fault by measuring earth potential relative to battery voltage.
Float Voltage: Provides monitoring and alarming of float voltage at the battery positive and negative terminals to ensure correct float voltage is being applied.
String Continuity: Monitors the precise float current in the battery by accurately measuring the potential difference across the cell interconnections, enabling reliable detection if the battery has a continuity fault.
Intercell and Terminal Connection Resistance: Provides monitoring and alarming of battery terminal resistance and each intercell connection resistance as independent values.
Internal Ohmic Value & Float Current: Provides monitoring and alarming of each cell’s internal resistance against an established baseline.
Electrolyte Level: Provides alarming and identification of low electrolyte level for every cell with infrared electrolyte level monitor (“ ELM”) sensors.
If any of the monitored values exceed the expected limit, a Company battery SME is consulted to determine if further monitoring is necessary or if the battery and charger need to be removed from service for off-line testing. Once offline testing and evaluation of the battery is complete, a decision is made to either repair or replace the battery.
Please see the Company’s response to STF-WG-2-29 part ‘e’.
No, condition-based maintenance (“CBM”) tools cannot determine the expected life of substation equipment. CBM is a maintenance strategy that monitors the real-time condition of an asset to determine what type of maintenance may need to be performed on the asset. These tools will enhance the reliability of substation assets and reduce O&M expenses through the proactive monitoring of the health of certain substation equipment.
It is important to note that CBM tools are intended for use on substation equipment that is within its industry expected life. Traditional maintenance practices have allowed the Company to extend the life of equipment beyond its industry expected life. Due to being in the beginning stages of CBM deployment on substation equipment across the system, it is yet to be determined if CBM tools can be used to extend the life of substation equipment beyond industry standards.

question:
Please refer to the Company's response to DR STF-REC-1-7-d. The latter part of the response states that “For these reasons, the Grid Investment Plan is deploying capital into the transmission system for assets that have a higher risk of failure due to their age.”
Describe how the failure risk is derived to determine if a transmission line needs to be rebuilt.
What are the criteria for prioritizing transmission line rebuilds based on such risk assessments?
Are the results of CBM tools used, in any way, to determine whether a transmission line needs to be upgraded, reconductored or rebuilt? If so, please provide the CBM tool outputs for such transmission line projects.
response:
Based on the Company’s operational experience and common understanding, the likelihood of failure for transmission line assets included in the Grid Investment Plan increases as the asset ages beyond its expected life. The underlying premise of the Grid Investment Plan is to proactively replace aging equipment to maintain reliability before aged transmission line assets begin to fail across the system.
The basis for transmission projects included in the Grid Investment Plan is the age of assets identified for replacement. Several factors are considered when prioritizing all transmission project packages within the Grid Investment Plan. These factors include the operational feasibility associated with the location and timing of project construction, the criticality of the line to a particular area of the system, and the impact of project construction on other planned or existing maintenance work. Project prioritization is continually refined through the deconfliction of projects between the Grid Investment Plan and other Capital Maintenance work. This review ensures the continuation of efficient investment and operational decisions across the transmission system with respect to implementation of the Grid Investment Plan.
CBM software and tools are not yet utilized in the monitoring of the health of transmission line assets.

For each substation power transformer replacement between January 1, 2018 and June 30, 2022 identify the substation power transformer replaced, gross plant-in-service and accumulated depreciation balances at time of replacement (retirement), years of service at time of replacement and capital expenditure to replace.
For each substation power transformer replacement between January 1, 2018 and June 30, 2022 provide the actual operating performance data and testing data of the substation power transformer used to justify the replacement. Please explain how this data was used to support the Company’s decision to replace.
response:
“Nearing end-of-life” describes when a piece of power equipment is beyond industry expected life and nearing Company expected life. Although the equipment is still performing its intended function, it may be performing that function with less efficiency or with less operational margin to withstand operational stresses, due to age-related degradation.
Please see the Company’s response to STF-WG-1-27 part (d).
Transformer replacements included in the Grid Investment Plan are based on the age of a transformer, with replacement being considered when the transformer has exceeded Company standards for expected life. It is important to note that through robust and comprehensive maintenance work, the Company has routinely extended the life of transformers beyond industry expected life. Transformers that will be greater than 50 years old by the end of the Grid Investment Plan period are eligible for replacement within the Grid Investment Plan. Without transformer replacement through the plan, the percentage of transformers that would reach the Company expected life by the end of the Grid Investment Plan period would more than double as compared to the state of the system when the plan was approved by the Commission in 2019. The Grid Investment Plan is designed to decrease risks to customers due to an expanding number of transformers that are or will be beyond Company expected life by 2031.
Please see the response to part (c) above. Although the transformers targeted for replacement as part of the Grid Investment Plan may still perform their intended function, they may be performing that function with less efficiency or with less operational margin to withstand operational stresses, due to age-related degradation. Therefore, the Company has deemed it appropriate to replace such transformers that have exceeded or will exceed Company standards for expected life by the end of the Grid Investment Plan period.
The Company has not performed a benefit-cost analysis for Grid Investment Plan transmission investments. As stated in the response to part (c) above, the Company’s transmission investment is based upon the age of the assets, with replacements occurring when transformers have exceeded or will exceed Company standards for expected life by the end of the Grid Investment Plan period. This transmission investment is aimed at avoiding increased equipment failures, higher maintenance costs, and higher replacement costs.
As of August 2022, no substation transformer replacements as part of the Grid Investment Plan have completed construction. Therefore, the Company has not yet recognized transformer retirements related to these projects.

question:
Refer to the Company’s response to Docket 44280 STF-WG-1-48 (b) and the associated TS Attachment. Staff notes that spot tree trimming/vegetation management is not listed as a WPF program remediation measure. In the experience of Staff's experts, a WPF program that does not employ spot tree trimming/vegetation management, particularly for a utility like GPC, for which a very significant percentage of outages involve vegetation or tree contact (per the responses to STF-WG-1-30) would make GPC unique.
Confirm that spot tree trimming/vegetation management is not employed as a WPF program remediation, and explain why not. If this cannot be confirmed, please explain why spot tree trimming/vegetation management was not listed in the response to STF-WG-1-48 (b).
Describe how the GPC regions identify the need for, and call upon, specialists to complete spot tree trimming/vegetation management when needed.
Tab STF-WG-1-48 a-b indicates a significant amount of O&M spending for WPF program remediation 2017-2021. Confirm that these are largely spot tree trimming/vegetation management expenses. If this cannot be confirmed, please describe what types of spending these significant O&M amounts represent.
Tab STF-WG-1-48 f lists 15 circuits identified for attention in the WPF program that received an undergrounding package.  For each of these, explain why undergrounding was employed instead of all other measures including spot tree trimming/vegetation management.
response:
While the Company does employ spot vegetation management in conjunction with its worst performing feeder (“WPF”) program, it was not listed as a remediation project type in the Company’s response to STF-WG-1-48 part (b) because spot tree trimming is targeted to relatively few locations on select projects within the WPF program. The bulk of the Company’s vegetation management activity is carried out within its routine vegetation management programs.
When Company field personnel identify a potential need for reactive vegetation management, information such as location, proximity to conductors, and the nature of the threat is provided to a utility arborist for evaluation. Utility arborists also receive customer reports of threatening vegetation conditions. The utility arborist then assesses the condition and initiates any needed vegetation management activities to mitigate the risk. This includes activities such as trimming trees that are in such proximity to the conductor that they will not hold cycle, removal of dead or threatening trees, and removal of broken out or threatening limbs above or adjacent to the conductor.
A portion of the O&M spending provided in tab STF-WG-1-48 a-b is for spot vegetation management expenses but most of the O&M provided is for other incidental maintenance work. Examples of the types of incidental maintenance work typically undertaken on projects within the WPF program include fuse replacements to achieve feeder re-coordination, replacement of less than a complete set of pole fixtures, relocating existing protective devices along a feeder, and transferring existing assets on a pole to facilitate installation of a new protective device.
The undergrounding package within the Grid Investment Plan is applied to circuits that exhibit the poorest reliability performance, have the most outages due to vegetation or vehicles, and already have high vegetation management spend that has not reduced outages, as described in the Company’s response to STF-L&A-5-38 Attachment, Table I.2 in Docket No. 42516. As determined by the Company, the undergrounding package was applied to these circuits based on the reliability data available, which indicated that this was the best investment to address the underlying root causes of continued outages on those circuits. As mentioned in the Company’s response to STF-WG-2-16 part (a), routine vegetation management solutions are only effective temporarily. Many of the vegetation management-related outages that are experienced on the Company’s Distribution system are caused by sources off the right-of-way where the Company has no rights to trim. Please note, as described in STF-L&A-5-38 Attachment (Docket No. 42516), these investments were part of the overall distribution Grid Investment Plan that was determined to generate the overall lowest total cost to customers.

response:
i)  The Company’s subject matter experts (“SMEs”) determined that it was a design flaw to allow the steel stranded core of self-dampening conductor to be free and disconnected from the outer aluminum strands of the ACSR.  During vibration instances, the steel core actively moves within the aluminum strands. This active movement within the conductor allows for vibration energy to be dissipated and typical aeolian vibration damage to be reduced significantly.  Since the conductor and core are actively moving independently of each other, this causes wear over time within the conductor. The rust resistant coating of the steel strands typically wears away, leading to core corrosion and core failure.  Additionally, the core strands moving within the aluminum strands can cause fretting of the aluminum into a powder, which seals the conductor body. This causes the conductor to hold water from rain and condensation and excess moisture builds up in the conductor, which also leads to core corrosion and failure.  Due to the Company experiencing and becoming aware of self-dampening conductor failures on its system and other ITS participants’ systems, the Company contacted a recognized conductor expert in the utility industry (a principal for Utility Consultants) and a principal engineer for Southwire Corporation.  Both industry SMEs recognized the self-dampening conductor product as a popular utility conductor that was used in the 1970's across the United States and commented that their knowledge of the product would indicate a typical life expectancy of 30 years or less due to the issues described above.

question: Please describe the criteria the Company uses to schedule transmission facilities and associated station equipment for replacement/rebuild that can be simultaneously taken out of service without compromising the reliability of the power system for a given year, if the replacement / rebuild programs occur during spring and fall.

question:
In the T&D cross-examination of the Company's witnesses by PIA Staff, Mr. Robinson stated "There is no way to perform a benefit-cost analysis on that (pre-emptive equipment replacement)".  PIA Staff is aware of an approach to benefit-cost analyses called "Risk-informed decision support".  The general calculation of benefits in such an approach (to be compared to costs) is as follows:
Benefit (Avoided Customer Costs) = Likelihood of a failure that results in a service interruption (meaning not backed up/n-1 or n-1-1 not available) X Consequence of the service interruption (costs to customers of the service interruption).
Please explain why Georgia Power could not use such an approach in determining the incremental benefits of pre-emptive equipment replacement, such that those benefits could be evaluated in the context of the incremental costs to customers of pre-emptive equipment replacement to complete a benefit-cost analysis on the practice.
Please explain why Georgia Power did not use such an approach to evaluate the pre-emptive equipment replacement practice before implementing the practice as its multi-billion-dollar transmission investment plan.
response:
The Company does not dispute the existence of other economic analyses and cost-benefit analyses, including the “Risk-informed decision support” approach referenced in the question. However, the complexities of performing such an analysis on the Company’s transmission system make doing so impractical. Moreover, the results of such an analysis would be questionable, at best, due to the dynamic nature of the transmission system and the impact of a sudden change in one or more variables. Transmission system complexities that make such an approach impractical include the networked nature of the system and the number of components and factors that impact its operation. With this in mind, the “risk-informed decision support” method referenced in the question describes an analysis for an isolated component and an isolated outcome, which fails to reflect the realities of Georgia Power’s interconnected transmission system operations. Further, the “risk-informed decision support” method specifically ignores many variables such as:
The type of failure that could occur, either in a controlled manner or a catastrophic manner.
Damages that could occur to adjacent equipment when component failure occurs.  Incremental costs could be incurred when additional equipment needs to be repaired after suffering damage following a catastrophic failure.
Impacts to execution of additional capital work due to failures, resulting in delay, work stoppage, or cancelled projects.
Labor cost impacts when additional capital work is cancelled or stopped due to failures.
Major substation equipment supply chain lead times.
Major substation equipment inventory and stocking strategy and costs to account for the increased risks.
The need for and cost of generation redispatch due to loss of transmission elements.
Operational risks for higher percentages of assets past Company expected life, in which a higher percentage would indicate higher risks.
Due to the dynamic nature of the transmission system, several of the variables identified above are constantly fluctuating, leading a static cost-benefit analysis to result in uncertain conclusions that could be rendered obsolete or invalid at any given time because of constant changes in system conditions. As stated in the Company’s response to STF-WG-4-4 part (h), a controlled, programmatic approach that accounts for operational and supply chain challenges is the best risk management for aging transmission system assets. The Company opposes any approach that requires waiting until assets included in the transmission portion of the Grid Investment Plan fail before replacing them. Such an approach would increase risks to customers and transmission system reliability.
For the reasons stated in the Company’s response to STF-WG-7-2 part (a), it is neither practical nor advisable to perform a cost-benefit analysis, such as the “Risk-informed decision support” approach, for transmission investments included in the Grid Investment Plan. The Company used asset age to justify capital investment in each facility, as transmission investments focus on mitigating the risk of outages associated with a significant, growing number of assets that are approaching or will have exceeded their Company expected lives by the end of the Grid Investment Plan.  As mentioned in the Company’s response to STF-WG-2-25 part (b), the cost of replacing equipment after a catastrophic failure is 2 to 13 times the cost of replacing the equipment in a controlled/planned manner. This does not include additional costs from outages, the impact to projects that had already been scheduled, losses on the system, and redispatch of generation.

response:
As outlined in the 2019 Base Rate Case (Docket No. 42516) and 2022 Base Rate Case (Docket No. 44280), the Grid Investment Plan transmission investments focus exclusively on mitigating the risk of outages associated with aging assets and infrastructure. To that end, the Company used asset age to develop the transmission system investments. Accordingly, the Company did not select transmission investments for the Grid Investment Plan based on loading and capacity issues or historical reliability data.
The following attachments should be viewed with the facts and context outlined above in mind. Please see STF-WG-10-25 Attachment A for the requested substation information and STF-WG-10-25 Attachment B for the requested transmission line information. Additionally, there are several category responses entered as “N/A” or not applicable that are explained through footnotes in the attachments. A summary of the footnotes is provided below.
The transmission system is designed and operated differently than the distribution system, which is largely based on radial circuits. Transmission is a network system planned and operated in accordance with the NERC Reliability Standards such that lines and transformers may not overload for the contingency loss of other facilities in the network. Transmission facility ratings have been provided as the “Loading” parameters requested are not an applicable concept in Transmission due to the parallel power flows of a network system. Please refer to Sections A & B of the Technical Appendix Volume 3 of the 2022 GPC IRP in Docket No. 44160 for an overview of the transmission planning process.
In STF-WG-10-25 Attachments A and B, the Company does not track SAIDI and SAIFI as requested. Transmission and Distribution SAIDI/SAIFI calculations are performed differently.  Transmission System Average Interruption Frequency and Duration values are calculated on an aggregate basis, not by individual lines and transformers.
In STF-WG-10-25 Attachment B, for transmission line facilities, the Company documents the maximum allowable loading in Amps rather than MVA so the values provided are the line facility ratings in Amps. The Company does not have overload capacity ratings or overload duration limits for transmission lines. Additionally, neither synchronous nor inverter-based generation is directly connected to individual transmission lines. Generation on the transmission system is connected into generation interconnection substations, typically with multiple transmission delivery paths.

question: Refer to the Company’s response to STF-WG-10-26 above. In a MS Excel spreadsheet, please provide a list of any outages that occurred on the backup supply capacity. response: The Company interprets “backup supply” as equipment that will carry the load in the event of a failure on the transmission system. The transmission system is dynamic in nature, where sources could change depending on the system configuration at any point in time. Transmission equipment does not generally have a specified “backup supply,” as network power flows automatically reroute to all other electrical paths in the transmission network if transmission equipment is out of service. In transmission operations planning and in real-time operations, the Company assesses N-1 and other contingencies to identify transmission constraints and adjusts the power system, as needed, to maintain reliable operations consistent with the NERC reliability standards. Keeping in mind that the “backup supply” that would serve as a redundant power source in the event of a failure changes dynamically, it is not possible to provide a list of outages that occurred on the “backup supply capacity,” It is important to note that each occurrence of an outage on major transmission equipment, such as transformers that are approaching or beyond the Company’s expected life, reduces the reliability of the system and often cancels planned/ongoing work on other portions of the system, which has negative impacts to cost and reliability.

question: In projects that have the phrase ‘… by the end of the plan’ in the justification, is this referring to 2025? 2031? If 2031, explain what equipment or other factors are triggering such a lead time.
response:
The phrase “by the end of the plan” refers to the end date of the Grid Investment Plan as presented in the 2019 Base Rate Case, which is 2031. As mentioned in the Company’s response to STF-WG-9-3 subpart (c), the Company intends to extend the Grid Investment Plan beyond 2031 to comply with the Commission’s Order in the 2022 Base Rate Case to reduce the overall plan spending by 40% during the current 3-year Alternate Rate Plan period. Although the Company intends to extend the plan, 2031 remains the benchmark for the project justifications included in STF-WG-9-3 Attachments B and C.
The significant number of transmission assets approaching or exceeding their Company expected life by 2031 underscores the need for transmission investment through the Grid Investment Plan.  This investment is essential due to the heightened risk of failure as assets age beyond their expected life. Further, investment is necessary to prevent transmission system reliability deterioration across the system. Having an increased number of assets nearing or past expected life also presents both operational and supply chain challenges should a failure occur, as the lead time for equipment has extended significantly in recent years (e.g., 3-5 years for substation transformers and breakers). The Grid Investment Plan provides a structured, programmatic approach to replacing aging transmission assets in a way that accounts for these considerations.

question:
Refer to the Company’s response to STF-WG-9-3, which states: “All projects included in the Grid Investment Plan are critical to improving reliability; however, to comply with the Commission’s Order in the 2022 Base Rate Case to reduce the overall plan spending by 40%, the Company considered several factors to prioritize the distribution projects in this rate case period in order to maximize work efficiency and reliability benefits to customers.”
Please provide the definition of the use of the word “critical” and the basis for the determination that “All projects included in the Grid Investment Plan are critical to improving reliability.”
Please explain the differences between grid capital spending that is critical to improving reliability and grid capital spending that is immediately required for safe and reliable service.  Please provide examples of circumstances and equipment installed for each of these two types of capital spending.
Provide a list of the types of equipment that are to be replaced under the Grid Investment Plan.
Refer to the list of equipment types provided in response to subpart (c).  For each type of equipment listed, provide a list of equipment failures, with dates, resulting in Customer Interruptions (CI) and Customer Minutes of Interruption (CMI) from 2017 through 2023.  For each equipment failure resulting in CI and CMI listed, provide the CI and CMI.
response:
In STF-WG-9-3 subpart (a), the phrase “less critical” was used to ask the Company how it identified the distribution projects to be deferred. The Company understood the phrase “less critical” to mean less vital. In response to that phrase, the Company stated that there are no projects that are less critical, or less vital, to improving reliability than others. The Company affirms that all projects included in the Grid Investment Plan are reasonable, appropriate, and necessary, pursuant to the Plan’s strategy and rationale, as outlined in STF-REC-1-1.
The immediate requirement for distribution investments under the Grid Investment Plan is not necessarily driven by an urgency to maintain safe service. The Company’s electrical system provides safe service in its current configuration. Distribution investments under the Grid Investment Plan are being made to improve reliability through investment in underperforming feeders on the system.
It is important to note that replacing equipment is not a driver of the distribution portion of the Grid Investment Plan. Equipment is replaced, as necessary, to implement the investment packages outlined in the Company’s response to STF-REC-1-1.  The types of equipment that may be replaced to implement these investment packages include line devices, wires, poles, and framing hardware, as noted in column H of STF-WG-9-1 Attachment A, previously filed by the Company in STF-WG-9-1.
The Company does not systematically track the type of equipment that fails on the distribution system. Please see STF-WG-1-30 Attachments F, G, H, I, and J, previously provided by the Company in STF-WG-1-30, for outages labeled as equipment failure (filter column L) and their resulting CIs and CMIs from 2017-2021, respectively.

question:
Refer to the Company’s response to STF-WG-9-3, which states: “Additionally, consideration was given for projects that contained related capital investment drivers, such as enhanced system reliability, the prevention of equipment failures and high replacement costs, and compliance with NERC reliability standards.”
Provide two examples that “contained related capital investment drivers” for
Enhanced system reliability
Prevention of equipment failures and high replacement costs
Compliance with NERC reliability standards
For each example of “enhanced system reliability” listed, provide all studies that were performed, including all data and sources of data, indicating that reduction in (CI) and (CMI) justify the expenditures.
For each example of “equipment failures and high replacement costs” listed, provide the analysis including equipment failure data, and cost data, including sources of data, which shows that improvement in equipment failures will provide dollar value to rate payers in excess of cost to rate payers.
For each example of “compliance with NERC reliability standards” provide the NERC standard to which the project will bring the equipment into compliance with.  Indicate if the equipment was out of compliance prior to the proposed work, and whether the standard requires retroactive application to existing construction or not.
response:
For the Transmission portion of the Grid Investment Plan (GIP), the Company used the age of the assets as the driver for inclusion in the plan. In response to STF-WG-9-3 subparts (c) and (e), the Company explained the criteria used to determine the Transmission projects selected for deferral from the 2023-2025 GIP to comply with the Commission’s Order to reduce GIP spending by 40%. In addition to qualifying age of assets, if a project contained secondary capital investment drivers, such as enhanced system reliability, the prevention of equipment failures and high replacement costs, or compliance with NERC reliability standards, then the project was considered for deferral from the 2023-2025 plan in the GIP.
i.)  Example 1 – Transmission structures on a transmission line are not only beyond or approaching their Company expected life, but the transmission line has also been identified as needing to be reconductored due to additional loading in the area.
Example 2 – Transmission conductor on a transmission line is beyond or approaching its Company expected life.  Instead of replacing the conductor, a larger area solution could be evaluated to solve multiple reliability issues in the area.
ii.)  Example 1 – An LTC transformer is not only beyond or approaching its Company expected life, but it has been identified for potential replacement due to being prone to failure, cost to repair, and lack of support from the manufacturer.
Example 2 – A breaker is not only beyond or approaching its Company expected life, but it has been identified for potential replacement due to being prone to failure, cost to repair, and lack of support from the manufacturer.
iii.)  Example 1 – During routine transmission planning studies, a transmission circuit's facility rating is exceeded by a single contingency event, such as the loss of a transmission circuit. This could necessitate a project to reconductor the overloaded circuit.
Example 2 – During routine transmission planning studies, a transmission circuit's facility rating is exceeded by a multiple contingency event, such as the loss of a generator unit and the loss of a transmission circuit. This could necessitate a project to rebuild the overloaded circuit.
b.    The example scenarios in subpart (a)(i) above could require transmission planning or area planning studies.  However, it is important to note that the Company does not use CI or CMI to determine transmission system reliability, thus no prospective studies would be performed to indicate reduction to CI or CMI.
c.    As stated in the Company’s response to STF-WG-11-8 subpart (c), the Company has not performed a cost-benefit analysis for transmission investments.  Replacing equipment that is approaching or beyond its Company expected life will prevent an escalation in equipment failures throughout the system.  This approach will also avert higher maintenance costs and avoid increased replacement costs should catastrophic failures occur.
d.  Please see Section B of Technical Appendix Volume 3 in Georgia Power’s 2022 Integrated Resource Plan in Docket No. 44160 for the applicable NERC reliability standards.  Transmission planning studies and their associated projects are finalized prior to being considered non-compliant, in accordance with the referenced NERC compliance standards. This ensures that transmission facilities remain in compliance.
